meta.title: YAML & JSON, from the grammar up

lessons.title: Two formats, one data model
lessons.summary: JSON and YAML both describe trees of maps, lists, and scalars. Learn that model first and the syntax becomes notation for it.
objectives: Name the six kinds of value that JSON can hold
Write the same small tree in JSON, YAML block style, and YAML flow style
Explain why a valid JSON document is also a valid YAML 1.2 document
Run the course helpers yaml2json and json2yaml and read their output

further.title: RFC 8259, The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

lessons.pitfall: "YAML is a superset of JSON" is true for YAML 1.2. Many tools still load YAML 1.1 (PyYAML is one), and under 1.1 a few JSON inputs read differently. Lesson 11 shows the cases. When someone says "it is just YAML", ask which version their parser implements.
lessons.markdown:
You will meet these two formats everywhere a program needs settings or a message. `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, and every REST API you call speak JSON. GitHub Actions workflows, Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files, and OpenAPI documents are usually YAML. They look different. Underneath, they describe the same kind of thing: a tree.

## The tree underneath

Every JSON document is one value, and a value is one of six things:

| Kind | JSON example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| object | `{"name": "api", "port": 8080}` | Unordered set of name/value pairs. YAML calls it a *mapping*. |
| array | `[1, 2, 3]` | Ordered list. YAML calls it a *sequence*. |
| string | `"hello"` | Always double-quoted in JSON. |
| number | `8080`, `-1.5e3` | One number type. No separate integer or float. |
| boolean | `true`, `false` | Lowercase only. |
| null | `null` | The absence of a value. |

Objects and arrays are containers. They hold other values, including other containers, so a document can nest as deep as you like. The other four are *scalars*: leaves of the tree.

YAML has the same three building blocks: mappings, sequences, and scalars. It adds features JSON lacks (comments, anchors, several documents in one file, explicit type tags), but when a YAML file is loaded into a program, the result is almost always the same tree of maps, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and nulls.

That is the main idea of this course. **Learn the tree first. Treat the syntax as notation for it.** Most YAML bugs come from a gap between the tree the author pictured and the tree the parser built.

## One tree, three spellings

Here is a small service description, written three ways. The script saves each spelling to a file and converts it to JSON with the course helper `yaml2json`. The `cmp` lines at the end compare the converted output byte for byte.

```example
{"id":"one-data-model-01","title":"The same tree in JSON, YAML block style, and YAML flow style","script":"cat > service.json <<'EOF'
{"name": "api", "port": 8080, "tags": ["web", "public"], "tls": null, "debug": false}
EOF

cat > service.yaml <<'EOF'
name: api
port: 8080
tags:
  - web
  - public
tls: null
debug: false
EOF

cat > service-flow.yaml <<'EOF'
{name: api, port: 8080, tags: [web, public], tls: null, debug: false}
EOF

yaml2json service.yaml > a.json
yaml2json service-flow.yaml > b.json
yaml2json service.json > c.json
cat a.json
cmp a.json b.json && echo "block style and flow style: same tree"
cmp a.json c.json && echo "YAML block style and the JSON file: same tree"
","stdout":"{
  "name": "api",
  "port": 8080,
  "tags": [
    "web",
    "public"
  ],
  "tls": null,
  "debug": false
}
block style and flow style: same tree
YAML block style and the JSON file: same tree
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/one-data-model-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

Three things to notice:

1. `service.json` went through a **YAML** parser and came out unchanged. YAML 1.2 was designed so that JSON documents are valid YAML.
2. The *flow style* (`{...}` and `[...]`) is YAML's JSON-like notation. Inside flow style, YAML still lets you leave strings unquoted.
3. The *block style* uses indentation and `- ` for list items. This is what most YAML files you meet look like.

## Going the other way

`json2yaml` reads strict JSON and writes block-style YAML. Lesson 17 covers what can and cannot survive a round trip. For plain data like this, nothing is lost.

```example
{"id":"one-data-model-02","title":"JSON to YAML and back again","script":"cat > order.json <<'EOF'
{
  "id": 1042,
  "customer": {"name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com"},
  "items": [
    {"sku": "A-1", "qty": 2},
    {"sku": "B-7", "qty": 1}
  ],
  "paid": true
}
EOF
json2yaml order.json | tee order.yaml
echo "---- back to JSON, compared with jq -S (sorted keys) ----"
yaml2json order.yaml | jq -S . > round.json
jq -S . order.json > original.json
diff original.json round.json && echo "round trip preserved the tree"
","stdout":"id: 1042
customer:
  name: Ada
  email: ada@example.com
items:
  - sku: A-1
    qty: 2
  - sku: B-7
    qty: 1
paid: true
---- back to JSON, compared with jq -S (sorted keys) ----
round trip preserved the tree
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/one-data-model-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

A sequence of mappings, written `- sku: A-1` followed by `  qty: 2`, often trips people up. The dash starts a list item, and that item is a mapping with two keys. Indentation is how you can tell `qty` belongs to the same item as `sku`.

## The tools used in this course

Every example on this site was run by the build, and the stdout and stderr shown are what came back. The examples rely on a few commands:

- `jq`, the command-line JSON processor, used from lesson 6 on.
- `python3` and `node`, used where a language's own JSON library behaves in a way worth seeing.
- Four small helpers in this repository's `tools/bin/`, each a thin wrapper around a published library:
  - `yaml2json` and `yamlcheck` use the [`yaml`](https://eemeli.org/yaml/) npm package, a YAML 1.2 parser that can also be switched to YAML 1.1 with `--yaml-1.1`.
  - `json2yaml` uses `JSON.parse` and then the same package's `stringify`.
  - `schema-check` uses [Ajv](https://ajv.js.org/) to validate against JSON Schema draft 2020-12.

To run the examples yourself, clone the repository, run `npm ci`, and put the helpers on your `PATH`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pragmaticarun/yaml-json-course.git
cd yaml-json-course
npm ci
export PATH="$PWD/tools/bin:$PATH"
```

The [playground](/playground) runs the same `yaml` package in your browser if you just want to try a snippet.

```example
{"id":"one-data-model-03","title":"What a helper reports when the input is broken","script":"printf 'name: api\n  port: 8080\n' > broken.yaml
yamlcheck broken.yaml
","stdout":"broken.yaml:1:7: BLOCK_AS_IMPLICIT_KEY: Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings
broken.yaml:1:7: MULTILINE_IMPLICIT_KEY: Implicit keys need to be on a single line
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/one-data-model-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

The messages give `file:line:column` and an error code from the `yaml` package. They are also a first look at how a YAML parser reads indentation. `port` is indented under `name: api`, so the parser tries to treat `api` and the next line as one value, then finds a second `key:` inside it. The real mistake is the two spaces before `port`, which the message does not mention. Lesson 9 covers indentation in detail.

```example
{"id":"one-data-model-04","title":"The exit status says whether parsing succeeded","script":"printf '{"name": "api",}\n' > trailing-comma.json
echo "As YAML (yaml2json accepts this flow mapping):"
yaml2json trailing-comma.json
echo "As strict JSON (json2yaml uses JSON.parse):"
json2yaml trailing-comma.json
","stdout":"As YAML (yaml2json accepts this flow mapping):
{
  "name": "api"
}
As strict JSON (json2yaml uses JSON.parse):
","stderr":"trailing-comma.json: Expected double-quoted property name in JSON at position 15 (line 1 column 16)
","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/one-data-model-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

The last example sets up later lessons. YAML's flow style allows a trailing comma, so the YAML parser accepted the file. `JSON.parse` follows RFC 8259, which does not, so it rejected the same bytes and the script ended with exit status 1. "Valid JSON is valid YAML" does not run in the other direction.

lessons.title: The whole JSON grammar
lessons.summary: JSON is small enough to hold in your head. Learn what it allows, what it forbids, and why three parsers can disagree about the forbidden parts.
objectives: Write valid JSON for each of the six value kinds, including a top-level scalar
List the things people add to JSON that the grammar does not allow
Read the error messages that node, Python, and jq give for the same bad input
Explain why a lenient parser is a hazard when you are validating input

further.title: RFC 8259, The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

lessons.pitfall: A parser that accepts something the grammar forbids is not "being helpful". If service A validates with a lenient parser and service B reads the same bytes with a strict one, they can disagree about what the document says. The installed jq 1.6 below is lenient in exactly this way.
lessons.markdown:
The JSON grammar fits on one page of RFC 8259. That is a feature. Every language has a parser for it, and the format has almost no room for dialects. In practice dialects appear anyway, mostly at the edges of the grammar. This lesson maps those edges.

## What the grammar allows

A JSON text is **one value**, with optional whitespace around it. A value is an object, an array, a string, a number, `true`, `false`, or `null`. Older documentation says a top-level value must be an object or array. That was RFC 4627. RFC 8259 dropped the restriction, so `42` and `"hi"` are complete, valid JSON documents.

Whitespace is four characters: space, tab, line feed, carriage return. It may appear between any two tokens and nowhere inside one. Objects and arrays separate their members with commas, and objects join name to value with a colon. That is all of it.

The next script feeds the same top-level scalars to three parsers. `jq -c .` prints compact JSON, `node` uses `JSON.parse`, and Python uses `json.load`.

```example
{"id":"json-grammar-01","title":"Top-level scalars are valid JSON","script":"for text in '42' '"hi"' 'null' 'true' '[]'; do
  printf '%s\n' "$text" > doc.json
  printf '%-6s jq=%s' "$text" "$(jq -c . doc.json)"
  printf ' node=%s' "$(node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("doc.json","utf8"))))')"
  printf ' python=%s\n' "$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.dumps(json.load(open("doc.json"))))')"
done
","stdout":"42     jq=42 node=42 python=42
"hi"   jq="hi" node="hi" python="hi"
null   jq=null node=null python=null
true   jq=true node=true python=true
[]     jq=[] node=[] python=[]
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-grammar-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

All three agree. Note that `null` is a document too. A file whose entire content is `null` is valid, and a program that reads it must not assume it got an object.

## What the grammar forbids

People bring habits from JavaScript, Python, and YAML. Each of these is **not** JSON:

| Habit | Example | Why people try it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trailing comma | `{"a": 1,}` | Cleaner diffs when you add a line |
| Single quotes | `{'a': 1}` | Python and JavaScript allow them |
| Unquoted keys | `{a: 1}` | JavaScript object literals |
| Leading zeros | `{"a": 01}` | Zero-padded IDs |
| `NaN`, `Infinity` | `{"a": NaN}` | Floating-point results |
| Comments | `// note` or `/* note */` | Config files |

Run each one through all three parsers and look at what comes back.

```example
{"id":"json-grammar-02","title":"Six invalid inputs, three parsers","script":"cat > cases.txt <<'EOF'
{"a":1,}
{'a':1}
{a:1}
{"a":01}
{"a":NaN}
{"a":Infinity}
EOF
while IFS= read -r text; do
  printf '%s\n' "$text" > t.json
  echo "--- $text"
  echo "jq:     $(jq -c . t.json 2>&1 | head -1)"
  echo "node:   $(node -e 'try{console.log(JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("t.json","utf8"))))}catch(e){console.log("ERROR",e.message.split("\n")[0].slice(0,60))}')"
  echo "python: $(python3 -c '
import json
try: print(json.dumps(json.load(open("t.json"))))
except Exception as e: print("ERROR", e)')"
done < cases.txt
","stdout":"--- {"a":1,}
jq:     parse error: Expected another key-value pair at line 1, column 8
node:   ERROR Expected double-quoted property name in JSON at position 7 (
python: ERROR Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 8 (char 7)
--- {'a':1}
jq:     parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 5
node:   ERROR Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 
python: ERROR Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
--- {a:1}
jq:     parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 3
node:   ERROR Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 
python: ERROR Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
--- {"a":01}
jq:     {"a":1}
node:   ERROR Unexpected number in JSON at position 6 (line 1 column 7)
python: ERROR Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 7 (char 6)
--- {"a":NaN}
jq:     {"a":null}
node:   ERROR Unexpected token 'N', "{"a":NaN}
python: {"a": NaN}
--- {"a":Infinity}
jq:     {"a":1.7976931348623157e+308}
node:   ERROR Unexpected token 'I', "{"a":Infinity}
python: {"a": Infinity}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-grammar-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

Read the output line by line:

- The first three inputs are rejected by all three parsers. The messages differ in wording, but each points at a line and column, which is what you want when hunting a stray comma in a large file.
- `01` is rejected by node and Python, but the installed **jq 1.6 accepts it and prints `1`**. A leading zero is not allowed by the grammar, so jq is being lenient.
- `NaN` and `Infinity` are rejected by node. **Python accepts both** and prints them back. jq 1.6 accepts them too, but silently changes them: `NaN` became `null` and `Infinity` became the largest finite double, `1.7976931348623157e+308`.

That last result is the dangerous one. A value that JSON cannot represent went in, and a different, valid-looking value came out, with exit status 0 and no warning.

## Making Python strict

Python's `json` module accepts `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity` by default. The `parse_constant` hook is called for those three names, and you can raise from it.

```example
{"id":"json-grammar-03","title":"Forbidding NaN in Python with parse_constant","script":"cat > strict.py <<'EOF'
import json, sys

def reject(name):
    raise ValueError(f"{name} is not valid JSON")

text = sys.argv[1]
print("default:", json.loads(text))
print("strict: ", json.loads(text, parse_constant=reject))
EOF
python3 strict.py '{"ratio": NaN}' 2>&1 | grep -E '^(default|strict|ValueError)'
","stdout":"default: {'ratio': nan}
ValueError: NaN is not valid JSON
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-grammar-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

Without the hook the document loads; with it, loading fails with the message from `reject`. If you write a service that accepts JSON from outside, pass this hook. The same module can also write the invalid value: `json.dumps(float("nan"))` produces `NaN`, which strict parsers then refuse. Pass `allow_nan=False` to `dumps` so that you find out at the sending end.

## Comments

JSON has no comments. Crockford removed them on purpose, to stop people hiding parsing directives in them. Files such as `tsconfig.json` accept comments because TypeScript reads them with its own lenient parser (lesson [Config files](/lessons/config-files)), not because JSON allows them. The next script shows what the parsers here do with one.

```example
{"id":"json-grammar-04","title":"Comments are an error everywhere here","script":"printf '// the port\n{"port": 8080}\n' > commented.json
jq -c . commented.json 2>&1 | head -1 || true
python3 -c 'import json; json.load(open("commented.json"))' 2>&1 | tail -1 || true
","stdout":"parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 3
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-grammar-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

If you need a comment in data that must stay strict, the usual workaround is a key such as `"_comment"`, which the consumer is told to ignore. YAML has real comments, which is one reason people prefer it for files that humans edit (lesson [YAML structure](/lessons/yaml-structure)).

## Empty input is not a document

An empty file contains no value, so it is not valid JSON. Node and Python report an error. jq 1.6 prints nothing and exits 0, so a pipeline can carry on with an empty result and no failure. Check what your tool does before relying on its exit status to catch a truncated download.

```example
{"id":"json-grammar-05","title":"Empty input","script":": > empty.json
jq -c . empty.json; echo "jq exit: $?"
python3 -c 'import json; json.load(open("empty.json"))' 2>&1 | tail -1 || true
","stdout":"jq exit: 0
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-grammar-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

lessons.title: Strings, escapes, and Unicode
lessons.summary: A JSON string is a quoted run of Unicode characters with a short list of escapes. The surprises are in how languages count its length and what they do with bytes that are not valid text.
objectives: Write the JSON escapes and decode a \uXXXX escape, including a surrogate pair
Explain why a control character must be escaped inside a string
Predict why one string has a different length in Python and in JavaScript
Recognise a byte order mark and invalid UTF-8 and know which tools tolerate them

further.title: Python json module, character encodings and ensure_ascii

lessons.pitfall: "Length of a string" has three answers: bytes, code points, and UTF-16 code units. JSON does not pick one. Python counts code points and JavaScript counts UTF-16 units, so the same emoji gives different lengths in each. Never use a length check in one language to guarantee a limit enforced in another.
lessons.markdown:
A JSON string starts and ends with a double quote. Between the quotes can be any Unicode character except the double quote, the backslash, and the control characters U+0000 through U+001F. Those must be written as escapes.

## The escapes

| Written | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `"` | double quote |
| `\` | backslash |
| `/` | forward slash (allowed, never required) |
| ` ` ` ` `
` `` `	` | backspace, form feed, line feed, carriage return, tab |
| `\uXXXX` | the UTF-16 code unit with that four-digit hex value |

No other backslash sequence is legal. In particular there is no `\x41`, no `'`, and no way to break a string over two lines.

The script below stores one string that uses most of them, then reads it three ways. `jq -r` prints the raw string without JSON quoting. `jq -c` prints it as JSON again. `jq -a` prints JSON with every non-ASCII character escaped.

```example
{"id":"json-strings-01","title":"One string, three views","script":"printf '{"e":"caf\\u00e9 \\ud83d\\ude00 \\n tab\\t q\\" s\\\\ sl\\/"}\n' > s.json
echo "--- the file"; cat s.json
echo "--- jq -r (the decoded text)"; jq -r .e s.json
echo "--- jq -c (JSON again)"; jq -c . s.json
echo "--- jq -a (ASCII only)"; jq -a -c . s.json
","stdout":"--- the file
{"e":"caf\u00e9 \ud83d\ude00 \n tab\t q\" s\\ sl\/"}
--- jq -r (the decoded text)
café 😀 
 tab	 q" s\ sl/
--- jq -c (JSON again)
{"e":"café 😀 \n tab\t q\" s\\ sl/"}
--- jq -a (ASCII only)
{"e":"caf\u00e9 \ud83d\ude00 \n tab\t q\" s\\ sl/"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-strings-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

Compare the file with the `jq -c` line. The escape `é` turned into the real character `é`, and the pair `😀` became a single emoji. The optional `/` became a plain `/`. Writing the escapes and writing the characters are two spellings of the same string.

## Surrogate pairs

`\uXXXX` names a UTF-16 code unit, which is 16 bits. Characters above U+FFFF, such as most emoji, do not fit, so JSON writes them as two escapes: a high surrogate (`�`) followed by a low surrogate (`�`). Together they mean U+1F600. A decoder must combine them. A lone surrogate is not a character at all.

That history explains a famous inconsistency. Each example runs in its own empty directory, so this script recreates the same file first. It then measures the string in Python and in node.

```example
{"id":"json-strings-02","title":"The same string, two lengths","script":"printf '{"e":"caf\\u00e9 \\ud83d\\ude00 \\n tab\\t q\\" s\\\\ sl\\/"}\n' > s.json
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
text = json.load(open("s.json"))["e"]
print("python len:", len(text))
EOF
node -e '
const text = JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("s.json", "utf8")).e;
console.log("node .length:", text.length);
console.log("node code points:", [...text].length);
'
","stdout":"python len: 23
node .length: 24
node code points: 23
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-strings-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

Python counts code points, so the emoji is one. JavaScript's `.length` counts UTF-16 units, so the emoji is two. Spreading the string into an array walks code points, which brings node back to Python's answer. A length limit written in one language and checked in the other is a bug waiting for its first emoji.

## ensure_ascii

When Python writes JSON, `json.dumps` escapes every non-ASCII character by default (`ensure_ascii=True`). That keeps the output pure ASCII, which is safe over any channel, but it makes the text hard to read and larger. Pass `ensure_ascii=False` to write real UTF-8.

```example
{"id":"json-strings-03","title":"Python's ensure_ascii switch","script":"printf '{"e":"caf\\u00e9 \\ud83d\\ude00 \\n tab\\t q\\" s\\\\ sl\\/"}\n' > s.json
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
data = json.load(open("s.json"))
print(json.dumps(data))
print(json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False))
EOF
","stdout":"{"e": "caf\u00e9 \ud83d\ude00 \n tab\t q\" s\\ sl/"}
{"e": "café 😀 \n tab\t q\" s\\ sl/"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-strings-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

Both lines decode to the same string. jq goes the other way: it writes UTF-8 by default and escapes only when you pass `-a`, as the first example showed.

## Control characters must be escaped

A literal tab or newline inside a string is not allowed. The next script writes a document with a real tab character in the string and asks each parser what it thinks.

```example
{"id":"json-strings-04","title":"A literal tab inside a string","script":"printf '{"a":"x\ty"}\n' > ctl.json
jq -c . ctl.json 2>&1 | head -1 || true
node -e 'try{JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("ctl.json","utf8"))}catch(e){console.log("node:",e.message)}'
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
try:
    json.load(open("ctl.json"))
except Exception as err:
    print("python:", err)
print("python, strict=False:", json.loads(open("ctl.json").read(), strict=False))
EOF
","stdout":"parse error: Invalid string: control characters from U+0000 through U+001F must be escaped at line 1, column 10
node: Bad control character in string literal in JSON at position 7 (line 1 column 8)
python: Invalid control character at: line 1 column 8 (char 7)
python, strict=False: {'a': 'x\ty'}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-strings-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

All three refuse by default. Python's `strict=False` switch lets control characters through. It exists for convenience with sloppy producers, and using it means your parser accepts text that other parsers will reject.

## Encoding: UTF-8, no byte order mark

RFC 8259 says JSON exchanged between systems must be UTF-8. It also says implementations must not add a byte order mark (BOM, the bytes `EF BB BF`) and may choose to ignore one. Two real-world problems follow: files saved by some Windows editors start with a BOM, and files that are not UTF-8 at all sneak in.

```example
{"id":"json-strings-05","title":"A BOM and an invalid byte","script":"printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' > bom.json
printf '{"a":"\xff"}' > bad8.json
echo "--- BOM"
jq -c . bom.json
python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("bom.json")))' 2>&1 | tail -1 || true
node -e 'try{JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("bom.json","utf8"))}catch(e){console.log("node:",e.name)}'
echo "--- byte 0xFF inside a string"
jq -c . bad8.json
python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("bad8.json")))' 2>&1 | tail -1 || true
","stdout":"--- BOM
{"a":1}
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Unexpected UTF-8 BOM (decode using utf-8-sig): line 1 column 1 (char 0)
node: SyntaxError
--- byte 0xFF inside a string
{"a":"�"}
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 6: invalid start byte
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-strings-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

The results split. The installed jq 1.6 accepts the BOM. Python and node both refuse it, and Python's message tells you to open the file as `utf-8-sig`. For the invalid byte, Python raises a decode error, while jq 1.6 prints a replacement character (`�`, U+FFFD) and carries on. Silent replacement loses data, so a pipeline that must not alter its input should decode strictly.

A lone surrogate is another gap in the specification: `"�"` is grammatically fine, but it is not a valid Unicode string. Python and JavaScript both load it, while jq 1.6 rejects it with a parse error about a bad surrogate pair escape. Do not rely on any behaviour for that input.

lessons.title: Numbers, precision, and big IDs
lessons.summary: JSON has one number type and says nothing about its size or precision. What you get back depends on the language that reads it, and large integers are where tools quietly disagree.
objectives: Describe what the JSON grammar says about numbers and what it leaves to the reader
Show a 64-bit integer losing precision in node and jq 1.6 but not in Python
Explain why 1.0 and 1 may or may not survive a round trip
Choose between a number and a string for an identifier, and read big values with Decimal

further.title: Python json module, parse_float and parse_int

lessons.pitfall: The grammar lets you write any number of digits. RFC 8259 only advises that interoperable software should expect no more precision than an IEEE 754 double provides. A 19-digit ID that is fine in Python or a database can be silently rounded by a JavaScript client or by the jq 1.6 installed here. Send identifiers as strings.
lessons.markdown:
The number grammar is short: an optional minus sign, an integer part with no leading zeros, an optional fraction, and an optional exponent. `0`, `-12`, `3.14`, and `6.02e23` are numbers. `01`, `.5`, `5.`, `+1`, and `0x1F` are not (lesson [The whole JSON grammar](/lessons/json-grammar)).

There is **one** number type. JSON does not distinguish an integer from a float, or a 32-bit value from a 64-bit one. It also does not say how many digits you may use. The text `9007199254740993` is a legal number. What a program does with it is the reader's decision.

## Three readers, one document

The next script reads one document in jq, node, and Python and prints what each holds. The `id` is 2^53 + 1, the first positive integer that a 64-bit double cannot store exactly.

```example
{"id":"json-numbers-01","title":"One document, three number models","script":"cat > n.json <<'EOF'
{"id": 9007199254740993, "big": 12345678901234567890123, "f": 1.0, "e": 1E2, "pi": 3.14159265358979323846264}
EOF
echo "--- jq -c"; jq -c . n.json
echo "--- node"
node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("n.json","utf8"))))'
echo "--- python"
python3 -c 'import json; print(json.dumps(json.load(open("n.json"))))'
","stdout":"--- jq -c
{"id":9007199254740992,"big":12345678901234568000000,"f":1,"e":100,"pi":3.141592653589793}
--- node
{"id":9007199254740992,"big":1.2345678901234568e+22,"f":1,"e":100,"pi":3.141592653589793}
--- python
{"id": 9007199254740993, "big": 12345678901234567890123, "f": 1.0, "e": 100.0, "pi": 3.141592653589793}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-numbers-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

Read the three lines against the input:

- **node and jq 1.6** hold every number as a 64-bit double. `id` came back as `9007199254740992`, one lower than what was written, with no warning. `big` was rounded to the nearest double. `pi` lost its trailing digits in all three tools, because the digits after the 17th are beyond any double.
- **Python** reads a number without a fraction or exponent as an arbitrary-precision `int`, so `id` and `big` came back exactly.
- `1.0` and `1E2` have a fraction or exponent, so Python reads them as floats and writes `1.0` and `100.0`. node and jq print `1` and `100`, because for them the two spellings were always the same number.

Notice what this means for round trips. Python preserved the text of `id` and `big` because it treats integers specially, not because JSON promises it.

## Doing arithmetic with doubles

Double precision is a property of the arithmetic too, not only the parser.

```example
{"id":"json-numbers-02","title":"The same sums in node and Python","script":"echo "node:"
node -e 'console.log(0.1 + 0.2); console.log(2**53 + 1); console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER)'
echo "python:"
python3 -c 'print(0.1 + 0.2); print(2**53 + 1); print(float(2**53 + 1))'
echo "jq:"
jq -n -c '[0.1 + 0.2, 9007199254740993 + 0]'
","stdout":"node:
0.30000000000000004
9007199254740992
9007199254740991
python:
0.30000000000000004
9007199254740993
9007199254740992.0
jq:
[0.30000000000000004,9007199254740992]
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-numbers-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

`0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` everywhere, because none of these languages can store 0.1 exactly in binary. `2**53 + 1` is where they split. node's `Number` rounds it, and the constant `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` tells you the largest integer below which every integer is exact. Python's `int` has no such limit, but converting that value to `float` rounds it, as the last line of its output shows. jq 1.6 does the sum with doubles.

## Identifiers: use strings

Twitter's API famously returns each tweet ID twice, as `id` (a number) and `id_str` (a string), because JavaScript clients corrupted the numeric form. The lesson generalises: if a value is an identifier rather than a quantity, you never add or compare it by size, so a string loses nothing and cannot be rounded.

```example
{"id":"json-numbers-03","title":"An ID as a number and as a string","script":"cat > ids.json <<'EOF'
```

## Keeping exact decimals in Python

Python's `json` module lets you choose how numbers are built. `parse_float=Decimal` keeps the digits you typed, including trailing zeros, which matters for prices and measurements.

```example
{"id":"json-numbers-04","title":"parse_float with Decimal","script":"python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
from decimal import Decimal

text = '{"price": 1.10, "qty": 3}'
print("default:     ", json.loads(text))
print("with Decimal:", json.loads(text, parse_float=Decimal))
EOF
","stdout":"default:      {'price': 1.1, 'qty': 3}
with Decimal: {'price': Decimal('1.10'), 'qty': 3}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-numbers-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

`1.10` stays `Decimal('1.10')`. Writing a `Decimal` back out takes an extra step, because `json.dumps` does not know the type. Pass a `default=` function or convert to a string. Many teams solve the problem on the wire instead and send money as an integer count of cents, or as a string such as `"1.10"`.

## Out-of-range numbers

A document may contain `1e400`, which is a legal number that no double can hold. Readers handle it in different ways. The next script shows the three here.

```example
{"id":"json-numbers-05","title":"A number too large for a double","script":"echo '{"s": 1e400}' > huge.json
echo "jq:     $(jq -c . huge.json)"
echo "node:   $(node -e 'const d = JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("huge.json","utf8")); console.log(d.s, JSON.stringify(d))')"
echo "python: $(python3 -c 'import json; d = json.load(open("huge.json")); print(d["s"], json.dumps(d))')"
","stdout":"jq:     {"s":1.7976931348623157e+308}
node:   Infinity {"s":null}
python: inf {"s": Infinity}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-numbers-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

jq 1.6 clamps to the largest finite double. node reads it as `Infinity`, and `JSON.stringify` then writes `null`, because JSON has no way to write infinity. Python reads `inf` and `json.dumps` writes `Infinity`, which is not valid JSON (lesson [The whole JSON grammar](/lessons/json-grammar)). In each case a legal input turned into something else without an error.

lessons.title: Objects, duplicate keys, and ordering
lessons.summary: A JSON object looks like a dictionary, but the grammar is looser than any dictionary type. Duplicate keys, key order, and the difference between null and missing all behave differently from what you might assume.
objectives: Say what RFC 8259 requires, and does not require, of object keys
Show how four tools treat a duplicated key and how to reject duplicates in Python
Explain why key order cannot carry meaning, and where it still shows up
Distinguish a key set to null from a missing key in jq, Python, and JavaScript

further.title: jq manual (keys, has, the alternative operator //)

lessons.pitfall: RFC 8259 says object names SHOULD be unique and that behaviour on duplicates is unpredictable. "Unpredictable" means two systems can read the same bytes and disagree. If a duplicate could change a permission or a price, reject it explicitly instead of trusting every parser to pick the same winner.
lessons.markdown:
An object is a set of name/value pairs. The grammar requires the names to be strings. It does not require them to be unique, and it says nothing about order. The RFC's wording is that names **should** be unique. Software is free to do something else, and it does.

## Duplicate keys

The script below parses `{"a":1,"b":2,"a":3}` with four tools: jq, node, Python, and the course's `yaml2json` helper, which is a YAML parser reading the JSON.

```example
{"id":"json-objects-01","title":"One duplicated key, four tools","script":"echo '{"a":1,"b":2,"a":3}' > dup.json
echo "jq:     $(jq -c . dup.json)"
echo "node:   $(node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("dup.json","utf8"))))')"
echo "python: $(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.dumps(json.load(open("dup.json"))))')"
echo "yaml2json:"
yaml2json dup.json || echo "(exit status $?)"
","stdout":"jq:     {"a":3,"b":2}
node:   {"a":3,"b":2}
python: {"a": 3, "b": 2}
yaml2json:
(exit status 1)
","stderr":"dup.json:1:14: DUPLICATE_KEY: Map keys must be unique
","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-objects-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

jq, node, and Python all return `{"a":3,"b":2}`: the **last** value wins, and the key keeps the position of its first appearance. That agreement is a convention, and not one you can rely on in every library. The YAML parser takes the opposite view. It reports `DUPLICATE_KEY` with a position and the helper exits with status 1. YAML 1.2 requires keys to be unique, so a parser that rejects the duplicate is following its specification.

Python can also be made strict. `json.load` calls an `object_pairs_hook` with the list of pairs before it builds the dictionary, and that list still contains both entries.

```example
{"id":"json-objects-02","title":"Rejecting duplicate keys in Python","script":"cat > strict_load.py <<'EOF'
import json, sys

def no_duplicates(pairs):
    seen = set()
    for key, _ in pairs:
        if key in seen:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate key: {key}")
        seen.add(key)
    return dict(pairs)

with open(sys.argv[1]) as handle:
    print(json.load(handle, object_pairs_hook=no_duplicates))
EOF
echo '{"role":"user","name":"x","role":"admin"}' > req.json
python3 strict_load.py req.json 2>&1 | tail -1
","stdout":"ValueError: duplicate key: role
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-objects-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

The example is deliberately a security-shaped one. If one component reads `role` as `user` and another as `admin`, you have a vulnerability, and the usual cause is two parsers with different rules about the same bytes.

## Key order

An object is unordered, so no program should depend on key order. That does not mean order is invisible. Parsers preserve it differently, and diffs, hashes, and signatures all see the bytes.

```example
{"id":"json-objects-03","title":"Key order in jq, node, and Python","script":"echo '{"z":1,"b":2,"a":{"y":1,"x":2},"1":"one","0":"zero"}' > ord.json
echo "input:       $(cat ord.json)"
echo "jq:          $(jq -c . ord.json)"
echo "jq -S:       $(jq -S -c . ord.json)"
echo "node:        $(node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("ord.json","utf8"))))')"
echo "python:      $(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.dumps(json.load(open("ord.json"))))')"
echo "python sort: $(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.dumps(json.load(open("ord.json")), sort_keys=True))')"
","stdout":"input:       {"z":1,"b":2,"a":{"y":1,"x":2},"1":"one","0":"zero"}
jq:          {"z":1,"b":2,"a":{"y":1,"x":2},"1":"one","0":"zero"}
jq -S:       {"0":"zero","1":"one","a":{"x":2,"y":1},"b":2,"z":1}
node:        {"0":"zero","1":"one","z":1,"b":2,"a":{"y":1,"x":2}}
python:      {"z": 1, "b": 2, "a": {"y": 1, "x": 2}, "1": "one", "0": "zero"}
python sort: {"0": "zero", "1": "one", "a": {"x": 2, "y": 1}, "b": 2, "z": 1}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-objects-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

jq and Python write keys back in the order they were read. `jq -S` and `sort_keys=True` sort them, at every level, which is how you make two documents comparable with `diff`. node is the surprise: it put `"0"` and `"1"` **first**, in numeric order, ahead of the other keys. JavaScript objects order integer-like keys before string keys, and `JSON.parse` builds ordinary objects. Any order you saw in a JavaScript client for numeric keys is the language's, not the document's.

For stable output, sort keys before you hash, sign, or diff. Lesson [Converting between YAML and JSON](/lessons/converting) uses `jq -S` for exactly this.

## null is not missing

`{"a": null}` and `{}` are different documents. A key set to `null` exists. A missing key does not. Whether your language shows the difference depends on how you ask.

```example
{"id":"json-objects-04","title":"null versus a missing key","script":"echo '{"a": null, "c": 1}' > nul.json
echo "jq has(a), has(b):  $(jq -c '[has("a"), has("b")]' nul.json)"
echo "jq .a, .b:          $(jq -c '[.a, .b]' nul.json)"
echo "jq .a // dflt:      $(jq -c '[.a // "dflt", .c // "dflt"]' nul.json)"
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
d = json.load(open("nul.json"))
print("python d.get:       ", d.get("a"), d.get("b"))
print("python in:          ", "a" in d, "b" in d)
EOF
node -e '
const d = JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("nul.json", "utf8"));
console.log("node values:        ", d.a, d.b);
console.log("node in:            ", "a" in d, "b" in d);
console.log("node stringify:     ", JSON.stringify({x: undefined, y: null}));
'
","stdout":"jq has(a), has(b):  [true,false]
jq .a, .b:          [null,null]
jq .a // dflt:      ["dflt",1]
python d.get:        None None
python in:           True False
node values:         null undefined
node in:             true false
node stringify:      {"y":null}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-objects-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Reading `.a` and `.b` in jq gives `null` for both, but `has` tells them apart. Python's `d.get` returns `None` for both, while `in` shows which exists. In node, reading the missing key gives `undefined`, a value JSON cannot write, so `JSON.stringify` drops the key `x` altogether and keeps `y`. Notice also that jq's `//` operator replaces both `null` and `false` with its default, so `.a // "dflt"` treats a present-but-null key like a missing one.

Choose a convention for your own formats and document it. Some APIs treat `null` as "clear this field" and a missing key as "leave it alone", and that distinction is what makes partial updates work.

## Empty containers

`{}` and `[]` are valid values and are not `null`. They are what you get from an object with no members or a list with no items.

```example
{"id":"json-objects-05","title":"Empty objects and arrays","script":"echo '{"a":{},"b":[]}' > empty.json
jq -c '[(.a|length), (.b|length), (.a == .b), (.a == null)]' empty.json
jq -c '{"a": null} | del(.a)' empty.json
","stdout":"[0,0,false,false]
{}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-objects-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

Both have length 0, the two are not equal to each other, and neither equals `null`. The last line shows `del` removing a key: deleting `a` from `{"a":null}` leaves `{}`, a different document from `{"a":null}`.

lessons.title: jq basics
lessons.summary: jq is a small language for taking JSON apart. Learn paths, the iterator, pipes, select, and the options that make it usable in shell scripts.
objectives: Read a value with a path and iterate over an array with .[]
Combine filters with the pipe and keep matches with select
Handle missing fields with //, the ? operator, and the -e exit status
Pass shell values into a filter safely with --arg and --argjson
lessons.pitfall: A jq filter is not a shell string. Never splice a shell variable into the filter text, as in "select(.name==\"$name\")". A quote in the value breaks the filter, or changes what it does. Pass values with --arg, which hands them over as data.
lessons.markdown:
`jq` reads JSON, runs a **filter** over it, and prints the result. Every filter takes one input and produces zero or more outputs. Everything in jq, from selecting a field to building a report, is a filter combined with other filters.

The installed jq here is **1.6**. The examples were run on it, and the manual at jqlang.org covers newer versions too, so check `jq --version` when a feature from the manual is missing.

All the examples in this lesson use the same input, a small team description. Each script recreates it first.

## Paths and the iterator

A dot is the identity filter, and it prints its input, pretty-printed. `.team` reads a field. `.members[0]` reads an array element, and `.members[]` produces **every** element, one output each.

```example
{"id":"jq-basics-01","title":"Fields, elements, and the iterator","script":"cat > people.json <<'EOF'
{"team":"core","members":[
 {"name":"Ada","role":"lead","langs":["c","python"],"active":true},
 {"name":"Bo","role":"dev","langs":["go"],"active":false},
 {"name":"Cy","role":"dev","langs":[],"active":true,"email":"cy@example.com"}
]}
EOF
echo "--- .team";                 jq '.team' people.json
echo "--- .team with -r";         jq -r '.team' people.json
echo "--- .members[0].name";      jq '.members[0].name' people.json
echo "--- .members[].name";       jq '.members[].name' people.json
echo "--- slice [1:], -c";        jq -c '.members[1:] | map(.name)' people.json
echo "--- last element, -c";      jq -c '.members[-1]' people.json
","stdout":"--- .team
"core"
--- .team with -r
core
--- .members[0].name
"Ada"
--- .members[].name
"Ada"
"Bo"
"Cy"
--- slice [1:], -c
["Bo","Cy"]
--- last element, -c
{"name":"Cy","role":"dev","langs":[],"active":true,"email":"cy@example.com"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-basics-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

`-r` is **raw output**. Without it strings print with their JSON quotes (`"core"`), and with it they print as plain text (`core`), which is what you want to pass to another command. `-c` is **compact output**: one line per result instead of the indented layout. `.members[1:]` is a slice, like Python's, and a negative index counts from the end.

## Pipes and select

The pipe `|` sends each output of the left filter into the right filter. `.members[] | .name` is the same as `.members[].name`. The filter `select(condition)` passes its input through when the condition is true and produces nothing when it is false, so it works as a filter on a stream.

```example
{"id":"jq-basics-02","title":"Filtering with select","script":"cat > people.json <<'EOF'
{"team":"core","members":[
 {"name":"Ada","role":"lead","langs":["c","python"],"active":true},
 {"name":"Bo","role":"dev","langs":["go"],"active":false},
 {"name":"Cy","role":"dev","langs":[],"active":true,"email":"cy@example.com"}
]}
EOF
echo "--- active members";  jq -c '.members[] | select(.active) | .name' people.json
echo "--- active devs";     jq -c '.members[] | select(.role == "dev" and .active) | {name}' people.json
echo "--- sizes";           jq -c 'keys, (.members | length), (.members[0] | keys)' people.json
","stdout":"--- active members
"Ada"
"Cy"
--- active devs
{"name":"Cy"}
--- sizes
["members","team"]
3
["active","langs","name","role"]
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-basics-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

`{name}` is shorthand for `{name: .name}`. `keys` returns an object's keys in **sorted** order, not file order. `length` of an array is its element count.

## Missing fields and errors

Asking an object for a key it lacks gives `null`, not an error. Asking the wrong *kind* of value for a key or index, such as indexing a number, is an error. The `//` operator supplies a default, and `?` suppresses an error.

```example
{"id":"jq-basics-03","title":"Missing fields, defaults, and errors","script":"cat > people.json <<'EOF'
[{"name":"Ada"},{"name":"Cy","email":"cy@example.com"}]
EOF
echo "--- .email on each";     jq -c '.[].email' people.json
echo "--- with a default";     jq -c '.[] | .email // "none"' people.json
echo '{"a":1}' > num.json
echo "--- indexing a number";  jq '.a[0]' num.json 2>&1 || echo "(exit status $?)"
echo "--- with ?";             jq '.a[0]?' num.json; echo "(exit status $?)"
","stdout":"--- .email on each
null
"cy@example.com"
--- with a default
"none"
"cy@example.com"
--- indexing a number
jq: error (at num.json:1): Cannot index number with number
(exit status 5)
--- with ?
(exit status 0)
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-basics-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

The first command shows `null` for the entry with no email. The default operator replaced it with `"none"`. Indexing the number `1` with `[0]` is an error: jq prints `jq: error ... Cannot index number with number` and exits with status 5. Adding `?` swallows the error. The filter produces no output at all and the exit status is 0, which is convenient, but it also hides real mistakes, so use it deliberately.

## Exit status for scripts

By default jq's exit status says whether it could run, not what it found. With `-e` (`--exit-status`), jq exits with 1 when the last output was `false` or `null`, and with 4 when there was no output at all. That lets an `if` in a shell script test the data.

```example
{"id":"jq-basics-04","title":"Using jq -e in a shell condition","script":"cat > people.json <<'EOF'
[{"name":"Ada","active":true},{"name":"Bo","active":false}]
EOF
if jq -e '.[] | select(.name == "Zed")' people.json > /dev/null; then
  echo "Zed found"
else
  echo "Zed not found (jq exit status $?)"
fi
jq -r '.[] | [.name, (.active | tostring)] | @tsv' people.json
","stdout":"Zed not found (jq exit status 4)
Ada	true
Bo	false
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-basics-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

`@tsv` and `@csv` format an array as a tab- or comma-separated row. They are the safe way to print columns, because they quote and escape the values, unlike `echo "$a,$b"`.

## Passing values in

`--arg name value` binds `$name` to a **string**. `--argjson name json` binds it to a parsed JSON value, so numbers stay numbers. Neither needs any quoting inside the filter.

```example
{"id":"jq-basics-05","title":"--arg and --argjson","script":"cat > people.json <<'EOF'
[{"name":"Ada","role":"lead","age":36},{"name":"Bo","role":"dev","age":29}]
EOF
role=dev
jq -r --arg r "$role" '.[] | select(.role == $r) | .name' people.json
jq -c --argjson min 30 '.[] | select(.age >= $min) | .name' people.json
jq -n -c --arg n 3 '$n | tonumber + 1'
","stdout":"Bo
"Ada"
4
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-basics-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

The `-n` flag runs the filter with no input, which is useful when you only want to build a value. `--arg n 3` creates the string `"3"`, so the last line converts it before doing arithmetic.

```exercise
EOF
jq -r '.members[] | select(.role == "dev") | .name' people.json

```

```exercise
{"id":"jq-basics-ex02","title":"Default for a missing field","prompt":"For `[{"name":"Ada"},{"name":"Bo","nick":"bo"}]`, print each person's nickname, using their name when there is no `nick`.","hint":"Use `//` to give `.nick` a fallback, and `-r` to print plain text.","hint2":"","solution":"`.nick // .name` gives the nickname when it exists and is neither null nor false, and the name otherwise.","script":"echo '[{"name":"Ada"},{"name":"Bo","nick":"bo"}]' > nicks.json
jq -r '.[] | .nick // .name' nicks.json
","stdout":"Ada
bo
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-basics-ex02.sh"}
```

```exercise
{"id":"jq-basics-ex03","title":"Pass a variable safely","prompt":"The shell variable `who` is set to `Ada`. Find the person with that name in `[{"name":"Ada","age":36},{"name":"Bo","age":29}]` and print their age. Do not put `$who` inside the filter text.","hint":"Use `--arg` and refer to it as `$name` inside the filter.","hint2":"","solution":"`--arg name "$who"` passes the value in as data. The filter compares `.name == $name` and the shell never touches the filter text.","script":"who=Ada
echo '[{"name":"Ada","age":36},{"name":"Bo","age":29}]' > ages.json
jq --arg name "$who" '.[] | select(.name == $name) | .age' ages.json
","stdout":"36
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-basics-ex03.sh"}
```

lessons.title: Reshaping JSON with jq
lessons.summary: Build new objects, summarise arrays, rewrite values, and edit a file safely. These are the jq patterns that replace most throwaway scripts.
objectives: Construct new objects and arrays from an existing document
Summarise a list with map, add, group_by, sort_by, and reduce
Convert between objects and key/value lists with to_entries and from_entries
Update and delete values, and edit a file in place without destroying it
lessons.pitfall: jq has no in-place flag. Writing "jq ... file > file" makes the shell truncate the file before jq reads it, and jq then reads an empty input. The command still exits with status 0. Write to a temporary file and rename it over the original.
lessons.markdown:
Lesson [jq basics](/lessons/jq-basics) used jq to read values out. This lesson uses it to produce new JSON. The same input is used throughout: four orders, each with a customer, a total, and a list of items. Every script recreates it.

## Building new values

An object construction `{a: .x, b: .y}` makes a new object from parts of the input. An array construction `[...]` collects every output of a filter into a list. `map(f)` is shorthand for `[.[] | f]`.

```example
{"id":"jq-transform-01","title":"Object construction, map, and add","script":"cat > orders.json <<'EOF'
[{"id":1,"cust":"ada","total":30,"items":["a","b"]},
 {"id":2,"cust":"bo","total":15,"items":["c"]},
 {"id":3,"cust":"ada","total":55.5,"items":[]},
 {"id":4,"cust":"cy","total":10,"items":["a"]}]
EOF
echo "--- reshape each order"
jq -c '.[] | {id, customer: .cust, n: (.items | length)}' orders.json
echo "--- sum of totals";   jq 'map(.total) | add' orders.json
echo "--- ids over 12";     jq -c 'map(select(.total > 12)) | map(.id)' orders.json
echo "--- all items";       jq -c '[.[] | .items[]]' orders.json
echo "--- text";            jq -r '.[] | "\(.id): \(.cust) owes \(.total)"' orders.json
","stdout":"--- reshape each order
{"id":1,"customer":"ada","n":2}
{"id":2,"customer":"bo","n":1}
{"id":3,"customer":"ada","n":0}
{"id":4,"customer":"cy","n":1}
--- sum of totals
110.5
--- ids over 12
[1,2,3]
--- all items
["a","b","c","a"]
--- text
1: ada owes 30
2: bo owes 15
3: ada owes 55.5
4: cy owes 10
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

`{id}` is shorthand for `{id: .id}`. The expression `"\(...)"` is string interpolation, handy with `-r` for readable lines.

## Grouping and summing

`group_by(.key)` sorts an array and splits it into runs that share a key. Each group is an array, so you can summarise it with another `map`. `sort_by` accepts several keys, and a negative sign reverses a number.

```example
{"id":"jq-transform-02","title":"group_by, sort_by, and reduce","script":"cat > orders.json <<'EOF'
[{"id":1,"cust":"ada","total":30},{"id":2,"cust":"bo","total":15},
 {"id":3,"cust":"ada","total":55.5},{"id":4,"cust":"cy","total":10}]
EOF
echo "--- per customer"
jq -c 'group_by(.cust) | map({cust: .[0].cust, orders: length, sum: (map(.total) | add)})' orders.json
echo "--- same totals with reduce"
jq -c 'reduce .[] as $o ({}; .[$o.cust] += $o.total)' orders.json
echo "--- biggest first"
jq -c 'sort_by(-.total) | map(.id)' orders.json
echo "--- add on one-key objects does NOT sum"
jq -c 'map({(.cust): .total}) | add' orders.json
","stdout":"--- per customer
[{"cust":"ada","orders":2,"sum":85.5},{"cust":"bo","orders":1,"sum":15},{"cust":"cy","orders":1,"sum":10}]
--- same totals with reduce
{"ada":85.5,"bo":15,"cy":10}
--- biggest first
[3,1,2,4]
--- add on one-key objects does NOT sum
{"ada":55.5,"bo":15,"cy":10}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

`reduce SOURCE as $x (START; UPDATE)` folds a stream into one value. Here the start is `{}`, and `.[$o.cust] += $o.total` adds each order's total into the entry for its customer, creating it when it is missing.

Look at the last result. Using `add` on one-key objects *merges* them, so the later `ada` entry replaced the earlier one: `55.5` instead of `85.5`. `add` sums numbers and concatenates arrays, but on objects it merges. When you need a sum per key, use `group_by` or `reduce`.

## Objects as lists of entries

`to_entries` turns an object into `[{"key": ..., "value": ...}, ...]`, which you can filter and sort like any array. `from_entries` turns it back. `with_entries(f)` does the round trip for you, and `map_values(f)` changes every value.

```example
{"id":"jq-transform-03","title":"to_entries, from_entries, with_entries","script":"echo '{"a": 1, "b": 2}' > kv.json
echo "--- to_entries";    jq -c 'to_entries' kv.json
echo "--- filter by value"; jq -c 'to_entries | map(select(.value > 1)) | from_entries' kv.json
echo "--- with_entries";  jq -c 'with_entries(.value += 10)' kv.json
echo "--- map_values";    jq -c 'map_values(. * 2)' kv.json
","stdout":"--- to_entries
[{"key":"a","value":1},{"key":"b","value":2}]
--- filter by value
{"b":2}
--- with_entries
{"a":11,"b":12}
--- map_values
{"a":2,"b":4}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

Reach for `to_entries` whenever you need to filter an object by its keys or values. Most jq reports over a dictionary, such as "keys that start with `x_`", are one `to_entries | map(select(...)) | from_entries` away.

## Updates and deletes

`.path = value` sets a path. `.path |= f` applies a filter to the current value at that path. `del(.path)` removes one. Updates operate on a copy and print the result, since jq never modifies its input file.

```example
{"id":"jq-transform-04","title":"Update with |=, set with =, delete with del","script":"echo '[{"id":1,"total":30,"items":["a"]},{"id":2,"total":15,"items":[]}]' > orders.json
echo "--- double every total"; jq -c 'map(.total |= . * 2) | map(.total)' orders.json
echo "--- add a field";        jq -c '.[0].tags = ["x"] | .[0]' orders.json
echo "--- drop a field";       jq -c 'map(del(.items))' orders.json
","stdout":"--- double every total
[60,30]
--- add a field
{"id":1,"total":30,"items":["a"],"tags":["x"]}
--- drop a field
[{"id":1,"total":30},{"id":2,"total":15}]
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

## Slurping

By default jq runs the filter once per top-level value in its input. With `-s` (`--slurp`) it first collects every value into one array and runs the filter once. That turns a file of separate documents into something you can sum or sort (lesson [JSON Lines](/lessons/json-lines) builds on this).

```example
{"id":"jq-transform-05","title":"--slurp","script":"printf '{"n":1}\n{"n":2}\n{"n":3}\n' > lines.json
echo "--- without -s, once per value"; jq -c '.n' lines.json
echo "--- with -s, once overall";     jq -c -s '{count: length, sum: (map(.n) | add)}' lines.json
","stdout":"--- without -s, once per value
1
2
3
--- with -s, once overall
{"count":3,"sum":6}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

## Editing a file safely

Because the shell opens the output file before jq starts, redirecting onto the input is a mistake. The next script shows the failure, then the correct pattern.

```example
{"id":"jq-transform-06","title":"The truncation trap and the safe edit","script":"echo '{"name":"app","port":80}' > cfg.json
echo "--- the wrong way"
cp cfg.json wrong.json
jq '.port = 8080' wrong.json > wrong.json
echo "jq exit status: $?"
echo "wrong.json is now $(wc -c < wrong.json) bytes"
echo "--- the right way"
jq '.port = 8080' cfg.json > cfg.json.tmp && mv cfg.json.tmp cfg.json
cat cfg.json
","stdout":"--- the wrong way
jq exit status: 0
wrong.json is now 0 bytes
--- the right way
{
  "name": "app",
  "port": 8080
}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-06.sh","truncated":false}
```

The wrong version left a zero-byte file and no error. The safe version writes the new content beside the original and replaces it in one `mv`, which is atomic when both names are in the same directory. If jq fails, the `&&` stops before `mv`, and the original stays intact.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id":"jq-transform-ex01","title":"Order count per customer","prompt":"From `[{"cust":"ada"},{"cust":"bo"},{"cust":"ada"}]`, produce the single object `{"ada": 2, "bo": 1}`.","hint":"Group by the customer, then build a one-key object per group. Because the keys are different after grouping, `add` merges them correctly.","hint2":"","solution":"After `group_by(.cust)` each group has one customer, so the one-key objects `{ada: 2}` and `{bo: 1}` have different keys and `add` combines them into one object.","script":"echo '[{"cust":"ada"},{"cust":"bo"},{"cust":"ada"}]' > c.json
jq -c 'group_by(.cust) | map({(.[0].cust): length}) | add' c.json
","stdout":"{"ada":2,"bo":1}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-ex01.sh"}
```

```exercise
{"id":"jq-transform-ex02","title":"Keep only the string settings","prompt":"For `{"name":"app","port":80,"env":"prod","debug":false}`, print an object containing only the entries whose value is a string.","hint":"`to_entries`, `select(.value | type == "string")`, then `from_entries`.","hint2":"","solution":"The filter keeps the `name` and `env` entries and rebuilds an object from them.","script":"echo '{"name":"app","port":80,"env":"prod","debug":false}' > s.json
jq -c 'to_entries | map(select(.value | type == "string")) | from_entries' s.json
","stdout":"{"name":"app","env":"prod"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-ex02.sh"}
```

```exercise
{"id":"jq-transform-ex03","title":"Bump a version in place","prompt":"`package.json` contains `{"name":"app","version":"1.0.0"}`. Change the version to `1.0.1` in the same file, without losing the file if jq fails.","hint":"Write to a temporary file and use `&&` before `mv`.","hint2":"","solution":"Write the updated document to `package.json.tmp` and only rename it over the original if jq succeeded.","script":"echo '{"name":"app","version":"1.0.0"}' > package.json
jq '.version = "1.0.1"' package.json > package.json.tmp && mv package.json.tmp package.json
cat package.json
","stdout":"{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.1"
}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/jq-transform-ex03.sh"}
```

lessons.title: JSON Lines for logs and streams
lessons.summary: One JSON value per line turns a log or an export into something you can stream, grep, and append to. Learn the format, the jq and Python patterns for it, and what each tool does when one line is bad.
objectives: Describe the JSON Lines format and why it suits logs and large exports
Filter and summarise a .jsonl file with jq, with and without --slurp
Read a .jsonl file line by line in Python and node, reporting the line number of a bad record
Predict how each tool behaves when one line in the middle is not valid JSON
lessons.pitfall: A .jsonl file is not a JSON document. Parsing the whole file with a JSON parser fails after the first line. Tools such as jq that read a stream of values stop at the first line that is not valid, so one corrupt record can hide everything after it. Decide up front whether a bad line is skipped, reported, or fatal.
lessons.markdown:
A normal JSON file holds one value, so a parser has to read the whole file before it can give you anything. A log with a million events as a single JSON array is awkward: you cannot append to it without rewriting the closing bracket, and you cannot read the first record until the last byte arrives.

**JSON Lines** (also called NDJSON, newline-delimited JSON) fixes that with one rule: each line is a complete JSON value, usually an object, and lines are separated by `
`. Because a compact JSON value never contains a raw newline (lesson [Strings, escapes, and Unicode](/lessons/json-strings)), splitting on newlines is always safe. Appending a record is appending a line. `head`, `tail`, `grep`, and `wc -l` all work on it.

## Reading a stream with jq

jq already treats its input as a stream of values. A filter runs once for each one, and `-c` prints each result on its own line, so the output is JSON Lines again.

```example
{"id":"json-lines-01","title":"Filtering a .jsonl file","script":"cat > log.jsonl <<'EOF'
{"t":1,"lvl":"info","msg":"start"}
{"t":2,"lvl":"error","msg":"boom"}
{"t":3,"lvl":"info","msg":"end"}
EOF
echo "--- one line per record, errors only"
jq -c 'select(.lvl == "error")' log.jsonl
echo "--- a column of messages"
jq -r '.msg' log.jsonl
echo "--- collect everything with -s"
jq -s -c '{records: length, levels: (map(.lvl) | unique)}' log.jsonl
echo "--- shell tools still work"
grep -c error log.jsonl
wc -l < log.jsonl
","stdout":"--- one line per record, errors only
{"t":2,"lvl":"error","msg":"boom"}
--- a column of messages
start
boom
end
--- collect everything with -s
{"records":3,"levels":["error","info"]}
--- shell tools still work
1
3
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-lines-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

With `-s` (slurp), jq reads every record into one array first. That gives you `length`, `group_by`, and `add`, at the price of holding the whole file in memory. Without it, jq handles one record at a time, so memory stays flat on a very large file.

Pretty-printed objects are still valid input to jq, because it does not care about line boundaries. The format is a convention for *writers* and for line-based tools. A file written with an indented `jq .` is not JSON Lines, even though jq can read it.

## A bad line in the middle

Real logs contain truncated writes, stack traces, and stray text. Here is a file whose third line is not JSON.

```example
{"id":"json-lines-02","title":"jq meets a bad line","script":"cat > log.jsonl <<'EOF'
{"t":1,"lvl":"info","msg":"start"}
{"t":2,"lvl":"error","msg":"boom"}
not json
{"t":4,"lvl":"info","msg":"end"}
EOF
jq -c . log.jsonl 2> err.txt || echo "(jq exit status $?)"
echo "--- stderr"
cat err.txt
echo "--- slurp"
jq -s -c . log.jsonl 2> err2.txt || echo "(jq exit status $?)"
cat err2.txt
","stdout":"{"t":1,"lvl":"info","msg":"start"}
{"t":2,"lvl":"error","msg":"boom"}
(jq exit status 4)
--- stderr
parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 3, column 4
--- slurp
(jq exit status 4)
parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 3, column 4
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-lines-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

Read the output carefully. jq printed the first two records, reported a parse error that names line 3, exited with status 4, and **never printed the fourth record**. The parser cannot resynchronise after a syntax error in a stream, so everything after the bad line is lost. With `-s` it is worse: no records at all are printed, because the array is never completed.

If you cannot guarantee clean input, read the file as plain text with `-R` (`--raw-input`) and decode each line yourself with `fromjson`. Wrapping it in `try` lets you decide what happens to a failure.

```example
{"id":"json-lines-03","title":"Skipping or reporting bad lines in jq","script":"cat > log.jsonl <<'EOF'
{"t":1,"lvl":"info","msg":"start"}
{"t":2,"lvl":"error","msg":"boom"}
not json
{"t":4,"lvl":"info","msg":"end"}
EOF
echo "--- skip bad lines"
jq -R -c 'fromjson? | .msg' log.jsonl
echo "--- report bad lines in the output"
jq -R -c 'try fromjson catch "bad: \(.)"' log.jsonl
","stdout":"--- skip bad lines
"start"
"boom"
"end"
--- report bad lines in the output
{"t":1,"lvl":"info","msg":"start"}
{"t":2,"lvl":"error","msg":"boom"}
"bad: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 4 (while parsing 'not json')"
{"t":4,"lvl":"info","msg":"end"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-lines-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

The first command drops line 3 and carries on, so all three valid records produce output. The second keeps a marker for the bad line in the output stream, which is easier to audit. Both read all four lines, unlike the plain version.

## The same job in Python and node

In a general-purpose language you control the loop, so you can number the lines and decide for each failure. Python's file object yields one line at a time, which keeps memory low.

```example
{"id":"json-lines-04","title":"Line-by-line parsing in Python","script":"cat > log.jsonl <<'EOF'
{"t":1,"lvl":"info","msg":"start"}
{"t":2,"lvl":"error","msg":"boom"}
not json
{"t":4,"lvl":"info","msg":"end"}
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json

with open("log.jsonl") as handle:
    for number, line in enumerate(handle, start=1):
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        try:
            record = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError as err:
            print(f"line {number}: skipped ({err})")
            continue
        print(f"line {number}: {record['lvl']}")
EOF
","stdout":"line 1: info
line 2: error
line 3: skipped (Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0))
line 4: info
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-lines-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Python reports the failure on line 3 and goes on to line 4. The same loop works in node when you split the text on newlines and call `JSON.parse` in a `try`. The next script also shows what happens if you hand the whole `.jsonl` file to a JSON parser as if it were one document.

```example
{"id":"json-lines-05","title":"Treating a .jsonl file as one document","script":"cat > two.jsonl <<'EOF'
{"a":1}
{"a":2}
EOF
echo "python:"
python3 -c 'import json; json.load(open("two.jsonl"))' 2>&1 | tail -1 || true
echo "node:"
node -e 'JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync("two.jsonl","utf8"))' 2>&1 | grep -m1 SyntaxError || true
echo "split and parse in node:"
node -e '
const lines = require("fs").readFileSync("two.jsonl", "utf8").split("\n").filter(Boolean);
console.log(lines.map((line) => JSON.parse(line).a));
'
","stdout":"python:
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Extra data: line 2 column 1 (char 8)
node:
SyntaxError: Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON at position 8 (line 2 column 1)
split and parse in node:
[ 1, 2 ]
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-lines-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

Both parsers read the first record and then fail on what follows it, with a message about extra data. This is the usual first symptom when a service is pointed at a `.jsonl` file and expects a JSON document.

## Writing JSON Lines

Writers must emit compact JSON and end every record with a newline, including the last. A file whose final line lacks the newline works in most readers, but `wc -l` will then count one fewer record than there are. Use `jq -c` or `json.dumps` with its default separators, and never pretty-print.

lessons.summary: Mappings, sequences, and nesting in block style. The indentation rules are short, and nearly every beginner error is one of three mistakes.
objectives: Write nested mappings and sequences in block style and predict the resulting tree
Explain how "- " counts toward indentation, and why a sequence may sit at the same column as its key
Spot the difference between a list item with a mapping inside and a list of plain strings
Read the error a parser gives for a tab, a mis-aligned key, and a mis-aligned list item

further.title: YAML 1.2.2 specification, chapter 6 (Basic Structures), indentation spaces

lessons.pitfall: A mis-indented list item is not always an error. If a "- " line is indented deeper than the previous item, the parser may read it as a continuation of the previous string, and the file still loads. The tree is wrong and nothing complains. Convert to JSON and look at the result whenever a list has an unexpected number of items.
lessons.markdown:
In lesson 1 you saw that YAML and JSON describe the same tree. This lesson is about the block notation that makes YAML look like YAML: no braces, no brackets, structure carried by line breaks and indentation.

## The three building blocks

A **block mapping** is a set of `key: value` lines that start in the same column. A **block sequence** is a set of `- item` lines that start in the same column. A value can be a scalar, or another mapping or sequence on the following lines, indented further.

```example
{"id":"yaml-structure-01","title":"Mappings, sequences, and nesting","script":"cat > app.yaml <<'EOF'
name: shop
owner:
  team: payments
  oncall: true
ports:
  - 80
  - 443
limits:
  cpu: 2
  memory: 512
EOF
yaml2json app.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"{"name":"shop","owner":{"team":"payments","oncall":true},"ports":[80,443],"limits":{"cpu":2,"memory":512}}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-structure-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

The `owner` key has no value on its own line, so its value is whatever block comes next, one level deeper. The `ports` key does the same with a sequence. There is no separate end marker: a block ends when a line appears at a shallower column.

## The indentation rules

The rules are short:

1. **Spaces only.** A tab cannot be used for indentation.
2. **Siblings share a column.** All keys of one mapping start at the same column. All items of one sequence do too.
3. **A child is indented more than its parent.** How much more is up to you, as long as you stay consistent within that block. Two spaces is the convention.
4. **`- ` counts as indentation.** The dash and the space after it take up two columns, and whatever follows the dash starts at the third.

The fourth rule explains the most common surprise. A sequence that is the value of a key is allowed to start at the *same column as the key*:

```example
{"id":"yaml-structure-02","title":"Indented and unindented sequences are the same tree","script":"printf 'a:\n- 1\n- 2\nb:\n  - 3\n' > seqs.yaml
cat seqs.yaml
echo "----"
yaml2json seqs.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"a:
- 1
- 2
b:
  - 3
----
{"a":[1,2],"b":[3]}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-structure-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

Both spellings are valid. Style guides disagree about which to use, so follow whatever the file you are editing already does. Kubernetes manifests often leave sequences unindented; GitHub workflows usually indent them.

## Lists of mappings

When a list item is a mapping, the first key can sit on the same line as the dash. The remaining keys line up under it, which is the column after `- `:

```example
{"id":"yaml-structure-03","title":"Lists of mappings, and a sequence inside a sequence","script":"cat > items.yaml <<'EOF'
- name: a
  size: 1
-
  name: b
  size: 2
EOF
yaml2json items.yaml | jq -c .
echo "---- a sequence directly inside a sequence ----"
printf -- '- - 1\n  - 2\n- - 3\n' | yaml2json | jq -c .
","stdout":"[{"name":"a","size":1},{"name":"b","size":2}]
---- a sequence directly inside a sequence ----
[[1,2],[3]]
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-structure-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

The first item uses the compact form and the second puts the dash alone. They produce the same kind of tree. The compact form is much more common because the dash points at the start of each record. A sequence directly inside a sequence also works, using two dashes on one line, as the last command shows.

## Flow collections inside block style

You can mix the two. A value in a block mapping may be written in flow style (`[...]` or `{...}`), which is handy for short lists:

```example
{"id":"yaml-structure-04","title":"Flow style inside block style","script":"cat > mixed.yaml <<'EOF'
tags: [web, public]
```

## The three common mistakes

```example
{"id":"yaml-structure-05","title":"Three indentation errors","script":"printf 'a:\n\tb: 1\n' > tab.yaml
printf 'a:\n  b: 1\n c: 2\n' > align.yaml
printf 'a:\n   - 1\n  - 2\n' > deeper.yaml
for f in tab align deeper; do
  echo "== $f.yaml"
  yamlcheck $f.yaml || true
done
","stdout":"== tab.yaml
tab.yaml:2:1: TAB_AS_INDENT: Tabs are not allowed as indentation
== align.yaml
align.yaml:3:1: BAD_INDENT: All mapping items must start at the same column
== deeper.yaml
deeper.yaml:3:1: BLOCK_AS_IMPLICIT_KEY: A block sequence may not be used as an implicit map key
deeper.yaml:3:3: MULTILINE_IMPLICIT_KEY: Implicit keys need to be on a single line
deeper.yaml:3:3: MISSING_CHAR: Implicit map keys need to be followed by map values
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-structure-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

The first file uses a tab, the second has a key at column 2 beside a sibling at column 3, and the third has a list item indented deeper than its neighbour. Each message gives a line and column and a short code from the `yaml` package. `TAB_AS_INDENT` and `BAD_INDENT` say what is wrong. The third message is less direct. The parser sees `- 1` start a sequence at column 4, then sees `- 2` at column 3, which cannot belong to that sequence and cannot be a key either. Its error names a block sequence used as an implicit map key. When a YAML error reads strangely, look at the indentation of the line it points at and the line above it.

The quiet version of the same mistake is worse. Here the second item is indented *one space further* than the first:

```example

yamlcheck quiet.yaml
yaml2json quiet.yaml | jq -c .

{"a":["1 - 2"]}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-structure-06.sh","truncated":false}
```

The file is valid, and `a` has one item, the string `"1 - 2"`. The extra-indented line was read as a continuation of the first item's text, folded onto one line with a space. Lesson 10 explains this folding rule. For now: if your list has the wrong number of items, convert it and look.
