lessons.markdown:
JSON has one way to write a string. YAML has five: plain, single-quoted, double-quoted, literal block, and folded block. They all produce the same kind of value, a string, but they differ in what they let you type. This lesson gets you from "I quote everything to be safe" to knowing when each style is the right tool.

## Plain, single-quoted, double-quoted

```example
{"id":"yaml-scalars-01","title":"Three styles for the same kind of value","script":"cat > styles.yaml <<'EOF'
plain: hello world
single: 'it''s fine'
double: "tab\there, caf\u00e9, \x41"
single_backslash: 'no\tescape here'
EOF
yaml2json styles.yaml
","stdout":"{
  "plain": "hello world",
  "single": "it's fine",
  "double": "tab\there, café, A",
  "single_backslash": "no\\tescape here"
}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-scalars-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

Read the output against the input:

- **Plain** has no quotes at all. The text is taken as written, with surrounding spaces trimmed.
- **Single-quoted** has exactly one escape: two single quotes in a row mean one quote. A backslash is just a backslash, which is why `'no	escape here'` came out with a literal `	`. JSON shows that as `\t`.
- **Double-quoted** supports backslash escapes such as `	`, `\xNN`, and `\uNNNN`, much like JSON strings. Use it when you need a tab, a newline, or a non-printing character.

Single quotes are the better default when the text contains backslashes, such as a regular expression or a Windows path. Nothing needs escaping except the quote itself.

A workable habit: write plain scalars for ordinary words and identifiers, single quotes when the text has backslashes or looks like something else, and double quotes only when you need an escape. Quoting is also how you tell the parser "this is a string" when plain text would be read as another type. That second use matters more than it seems, and lesson 11 is built around it.

## What forces quotes

A plain scalar is not just "anything". The parser treats some characters specially at the start of a value, and some sequences anywhere:

```example
{"id":"yaml-scalars-02","title":"Which plain scalars survive","script":"cat > forces.yaml <<'EOF'
colon_quoted: "a: b"
hash_quoted: "a #b"
inline_hash: a#b
comment_after: a #b
at_quoted: "@user"
EOF
yaml2json forces.yaml | jq -c .
echo "---- the unquoted forms ----"
for v in '@user' 'x: y' '- x' '[x' '*' '%x'; do
  printf 'a: %s\n' "$v" > one.yaml
  printf '%s  ->  ' "$v"
  yamlcheck one.yaml | head -n 1 || true
done
","stdout":"{"colon_quoted":"a: b","hash_quoted":"a #b","inline_hash":"a#b","comment_after":"a","at_quoted":"@user"}
---- the unquoted forms ----
@user  ->  one.yaml:1:4: BAD_SCALAR_START: Plain value cannot start with reserved character @
x: y  ->  one.yaml:1:4: BLOCK_AS_IMPLICIT_KEY: Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings
- x  ->  one.yaml:1:4: UNEXPECTED_TOKEN: Unexpected block-seq-ind on same line with key
[x  ->  one.yaml:2:1: BAD_INDENT: Flow sequence in block collection must be sufficiently indented and end with a ]
*  ->  one.yaml:1:4: BAD_ALIAS: Alias cannot be an empty string
%x  ->  one.yaml:1:4: BAD_SCALAR_START: Plain value cannot start with directive indicator character %
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-scalars-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

The first block shows quoting working. `a#b` is fine because the comment marker `#` only counts when a space comes before it, so `comment_after: a #b` is the string `a` followed by a comment. The second part runs each risky value unquoted and prints the first message. Each one fails: `@` and `%` are reserved indicator characters, `x: y` looks like a nested mapping, `- x` looks like a list item on the key's line, `[x` opens a flow sequence that never closes, and a bare `*` is an alias with no name.

The practical rule: quote any value that starts with one of ``@ ` * & ! | > % { [ ' "`` , contains `: ` or ` #`, or that you would not want read as a number, boolean, or null. The last case is the subject of lesson 11.

## Literal blocks: keep the line breaks

A `|` after the key starts a **literal** block. The indented lines that follow become the value, line breaks and all. This is what you want for shell scripts, certificates, and anything where lines matter.

## Folded blocks: join lines into paragraphs

A `>` starts a **folded** block. A single line break becomes a space, a blank line becomes a real newline, and lines that are indented *more* than the rest keep their break. It suits long prose you want to wrap in the source file.

```example
{"id":"yaml-scalars-03","title":"Literal and folded blocks","script":"cat > blocks.yaml <<'EOF'
literal: |
  line one
    indented
  line three
folded: >
  folded text
  continues here

  new paragraph
EOF
yaml2json blocks.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"{"literal":"line one\n  indented\nline three\n","folded":"folded text continues here\nnew paragraph\n"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-scalars-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

In the literal value the second line keeps its two extra spaces. In the folded value, `folded text` and `continues here` merged into one line, and the blank line became `
`.

## Chomping: controlling the trailing newlines

By default (called *clip*) a block scalar ends with exactly one newline, no matter how many blank lines follow it. Two indicators on the header change that:

- `|-` or `>-` (*strip*) removes the final newline.
- `|+` or `>+` (*keep*) keeps every trailing blank line.

An *indentation indicator* is a digit, as in `|2`. It sets the indentation explicitly, which you need when the first line of the content starts with spaces that would otherwise be taken as indentation.

```example
{"id":"yaml-scalars-04","title":"Clip, strip, keep, and an indentation indicator","script":"cat > chomp.yaml <<'EOF'
clip: |
  one newline
strip: |-
  no trailing newline
keep: |+
  keeps newlines


indicator: |2
    two extra spaces
EOF
yaml2json chomp.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"{"clip":"one newline\n","strip":"no trailing newline","keep":"keeps newlines\n\n\n","indicator":"  two extra spaces\n"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-scalars-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

`keep` ended in three newlines: the one that ends the line, plus the two blank lines. `indicator` begins with two spaces because the indicator `2` said the indentation is two columns and the line has four.

## Multi-line plain scalars

A plain scalar can also wrap across lines, using the same folding rule as `>`:

```example
{"id":"yaml-scalars-05","title":"A plain scalar that spans lines","script":"cat > multi.yaml <<'EOF'
multi: first line
  second line

  after blank
EOF
yaml2json multi.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"{"multi":"first line second line\nafter blank"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-scalars-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

The first break became a space and the blank line became a newline. This is how the quiet bug in lesson 9 happened: an over-indented `- 2` was read as more text for the previous item. Using a block style when text spans lines makes your intent explicit.

For how text turns into JSON strings and which escapes JSON has, see [JSON strings](/lessons/json-strings).

lessons.pitfall: Two programs can load the same YAML file and get different trees, because they implement different YAML versions. A library that follows YAML 1.1 reads `no` as false, `010` as 8, and `1:30` as 90. One that follows 1.2 does not. If a value must be a string, quote it, so the answer does not depend on which parser reads the file.
lessons.markdown:
JSON values carry their type in their spelling: quotes mean string, digits mean number, `true` means boolean. A YAML scalar does not need quotes, so the parser has to *guess* the type of an unquoted value from its text. The rules for guessing are the YAML **schema**, and there are two you will meet.

## Two sets of rules

- **YAML 1.2 Core schema** is what the `yaml2json` helper uses by default. It recognises `null`, `~`, an empty value, `true`/`false` in a few capitalisations, decimal integers, floats, and `0x` hex and `0o` octal.
- **YAML 1.1** has a larger set. It also treats `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, `y`, `n` as booleans, reads a leading `0` as octal, and reads `1:30` as a number in base 60. Some very widely used libraries still implement 1.1. PyYAML is the best-known example.

The helper takes `--yaml-1.1` to switch. Here is one file read both ways:

```example
{"id":"yaml-types-01","title":"One file, two schemas","script":"cat > t.yaml <<'EOF'
countries: [GB, NO, DE]
switches: [yes, no, on, off, y, n]
octal_looking: 010
explicit_octal: 0o10
duration: 1:30
version: 3.10
EOF
echo "== YAML 1.2 (default)"
yaml2json t.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== YAML 1.1"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 t.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"== YAML 1.2 (default)
{"countries":["GB","NO","DE"],"switches":["yes","no","on","off","y","n"],"octal_looking":10,"explicit_octal":8,"duration":"1:30","version":3.1}
== YAML 1.1
{"countries":["GB",false,"DE"],"switches":[true,false,true,false,true,false],"octal_looking":8,"explicit_octal":"0o10","duration":90,"version":3.1}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-types-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

Compare the two lines:

- **`countries`.** Under 1.1 the second item, `NO`, became `false`. This is the **Norway problem**: a list of ISO country codes loses Norway because `NO` looks like "no".
- **`switches`.** Under 1.2 only `true` and `false` are booleans, so the six words stay strings. Under 1.1 all six become booleans.
- **`octal_looking`.** `010` is 10 under 1.2 (a decimal with a leading zero) and 8 under 1.1. An octal literal in 1.2 must be written `0o10`, and in 1.1 that is not a number, so it stays the string `"0o10"`.
- **`duration`.** `1:30` is the string `"1:30"` under 1.2 and the number 90 under 1.1 (one minute thirty seconds, counted in base 60).
- **`version`.** Both give `3.1`. `3.10` is a float in either schema, and the trailing zero is not kept. A version that must read `3.10` has to be a string.

The version case is not a YAML 1.1 quirk. It follows from the number rule alone, which makes it a common source of bugs in CI matrices, where `python: [3.8, 3.9, 3.10]` loses the last one's identity.

A note on the word "guess". The resolution of types happens in the parser, before your program sees the data. By the time you hold a value in memory, nothing records whether the author wrote `no` or `false`, or `010` or `10`. A bug that comes from the wrong guess cannot be fixed afterwards in application code, because the information is already gone. It has to be fixed in the source file or in the parser settings.

## The key `on`

The same schema difference changes keys, not just values:

```example
{"id":"yaml-types-02","title":"A key named on","script":"printf 'on: push\nname: ci\n' > wf.yaml
echo "== YAML 1.2"
yaml2json wf.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== YAML 1.1"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 wf.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"== YAML 1.2
{"on":"push","name":"ci"}
== YAML 1.1
{"true":"push","name":"ci"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-types-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

Under 1.1 the key `on` became the string `"true"`, because JSON keys must be strings and the boolean `true` has to be spelled somehow. GitHub Actions workflows start with `on:`, so this is a known trap when you load a workflow with a 1.1 library. Lesson 18 returns to it.

## Nulls, empties, and special floats

```example
{"id":"yaml-types-03","title":"Null spellings and special floats","script":"cat > nulls.yaml <<'EOF'
tilde: ~
empty:
word: null
inf: .inf
nan: .nan
hex: 0x1F
plus: +12
exp: 1e3
date: 2024-01-15
EOF
echo "== YAML 1.2"
yaml2json nulls.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== YAML 1.1"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 nulls.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"== YAML 1.2
{"tilde":null,"empty":null,"word":null,"inf":null,"nan":null,"hex":31,"plus":12,"exp":1000,"date":"2024-01-15"}
== YAML 1.1
{"tilde":null,"empty":null,"word":null,"inf":null,"nan":null,"hex":31,"plus":12,"exp":1000,"date":"2024-01-15T00:00:00.000Z"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-types-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

Three spellings of null agree: `~`, nothing at all, and the word `null`. A missing value is `null`, not an empty string. If you want an empty string, write `''`.

Two lines of the output deserve care:

- **`inf` and `nan`.** Both schemas parse `.inf` and `.nan` into real floating-point infinity and not-a-number, but **JSON cannot represent either**. The helper's `JSON.stringify` step wrote `null` for both, so the output does not distinguish them from a true null. Treat that as a limit of converting to JSON, not as the YAML meaning.
- **`date`.** YAML 1.2 Core leaves `2024-01-15` as a string. YAML 1.1 has a timestamp type, so the library turned it into a date object, which appears in JSON as `"2024-01-15T00:00:00.000Z"`, with a time and a time zone that were never in the source.

## The fix: say what you mean

Quoting always gives a string, in any version. An explicit tag does the same:

```example
{"id":"yaml-types-04","title":"Quoting and !!str keep strings as strings","script":"cat > safe.yaml <<'EOF'
countries: [GB, "NO", DE]
code: !!str 010
duration: "1:30"
version: "3.10"
EOF
echo "== YAML 1.2"
yaml2json safe.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== YAML 1.1"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 safe.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"== YAML 1.2
{"countries":["GB","NO","DE"],"code":"010","duration":"1:30","version":"3.10"}
== YAML 1.1
{"countries":["GB","NO","DE"],"code":"010","duration":"1:30","version":"3.10"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-types-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Both parsers give the same result now. That is the property you want from config that other people's tools will read.

Many teams adopt a simple convention: quote every string that could be mistaken for another type, and run a schema check ([JSON Schema basics](/lessons/json-schema-basics)) so a value of the wrong type is caught on load, not in production.

lessons.title: Anchors, aliases, and merge keys
lessons.summary: Anchors let one YAML node be reused in several places. Learn what an alias means, what disappears when you convert to JSON, and why the merge key behaves differently depending on the YAML version.
objectives: Define a node with an anchor and reuse it with an alias
Explain why converting to JSON turns each alias into a copy
Use the merge key to share defaults, and predict which value wins
State which parsers merge `<<` and which treat it as an ordinary key
lessons.pitfall: The merge key `<<` is not part of the YAML 1.2 specification. It comes from a type defined for YAML 1.1. Many tools support it anyway, and many do not. A file that relies on `<<` can load as a clean config in one program and as a mapping with a literal key named "<<" in another, with no error in either.
lessons.markdown:
JSON has no way to say "this value is the same as that one". If two services share a configuration, you write it twice. YAML adds a feature for this: mark a node with an **anchor** and refer to it later with an **alias**. This lesson covers what that does, what it does not do, and the related merge key that many files rely on.

## Anchor and alias

An anchor is `&name` placed before a node. An alias is `*name`, and it stands for the anchored node.

```example
{"id":"yaml-anchors-01","title":"Define once, use twice","script":"cat > anchors.yaml <<'EOF'\ndefault_port: &port 8080\nweb:\n  port: *port\nadmin:\n  port: *port\nlist: &tags [a, b]\nother: *tags\nEOF\nyaml2json anchors.yaml | jq -c .\n","stdout":"{\"default_port\":8080,\"web\":{\"port\":8080},\"admin\":{\"port\":8080},\"list\":[\"a\",\"b\"],\"other\":[\"a\",\"b\"]}\n","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

An alias can refer to a scalar or to a whole collection. The rule is that the anchor must appear earlier in the file than the alias that uses it. A name with no anchor is an error. Check it with `yaml2json` here, because it is the conversion step that resolves aliases and reports the failure:

```example
{"id":"yaml-anchors-02","title":"An alias with no anchor","script":"printf 'a: *nope\\n' > bad.yaml\nyaml2json bad.yaml\n","stdout":"","stderr":"bad.yaml: Unresolved alias (the anchor must be set before the alias): nope\n","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

## Aliases become copies in JSON

In a YAML parser's memory, an alias can point at the *same* object as its anchor. JSON has no such notion, so on conversion every alias becomes a full, independent copy. The output above shows `"other": ["a","b"]` written out twice, once under `list` and once under `other`. The sharing is gone.

Two consequences follow:

- Converting YAML to JSON and back does **not** restore the anchors. The result is longer and has no reuse. See [Converting between formats](/lessons/converting).
- Anchors are a feature of the *file*. If your program loads the YAML and edits one copy, whether the other changes depends on how the library represents aliases. Do not count on either behaviour.

You can reuse a name. A later anchor with the same name replaces the earlier one for aliases that come after it:

```example
{"id":"yaml-anchors-03","title":"Re-defining an anchor name","script":"printf 'a: &x 1\\nb: *x\\nc: &x 2\\nd: *x\\n' | yaml2json | jq -c .\n","stdout":"{\"a\":1,\"b\":1,\"c\":2,\"d\":2}\n","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

`b` got 1 and `d` got 2. It parses, but it is a confusing thing to write.

## The merge key

Copying a whole mapping is useful, but the common need is "all of these defaults, with two changes". The merge key `<<` does that: its value is a mapping (or a list of mappings) whose keys are added to the current one.

The merge key is where YAML versions diverge, so the same file is read both ways:

```example
{"id":"yaml-anchors-04","title":"The merge key under YAML 1.2 and YAML 1.1","script":"cat > merge.yaml <<'EOF'\nbase: &base\n  retries: 3\n  timeout: 30\nsvc:\n  <<: *base\n  timeout: 60\nEOF\necho \"== YAML 1.2 (default)\"\nyaml2json merge.yaml | jq -c .\necho \"== YAML 1.1\"\nyaml2json --yaml-1.1 merge.yaml | jq -c .\n","stdout":"== YAML 1.2 (default)\n{\"base\":{\"retries\":3,\"timeout\":30},\"svc\":{\"<<\":{\"retries\":3,\"timeout\":30},\"timeout\":60}}\n== YAML 1.1\n{\"base\":{\"retries\":3,\"timeout\":30},\"svc\":{\"retries\":3,\"timeout\":60}}\n","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Under YAML 1.1, `svc` got `retries` from `base`, and its own `timeout: 60` took priority over the merged 30. Under 1.2 (the helper's default) nothing was merged: `svc` has a key literally named `<<`, whose value is a copy of `base`. No error is reported, which is why the pitfall above matters.

So what do real tools do? Support varies between libraries and between settings of one library. When you write a file that uses `<<`, find out what the program that loads it does, and test it, as this lesson does.

## Which value wins

With a list of mappings, earlier entries take priority. An explicit key in the mapping itself beats every merged one.

```example
{"id":"yaml-anchors-05","title":"Merge order and overrides","script":"cat > order.yaml <<'EOF'\np: &p {k: 1, other: 1}\nq: &q {k: 2, extra: 2}\nfirst_wins: {<<: [*p, *q]}\nreversed:   {<<: [*q, *p]}\nexplicit:   {<<: *p, k: 9}\nEOF\nyaml2json --yaml-1.1 order.yaml | jq -c '{first_wins, reversed, explicit}'\n","stdout":"{\"first_wins\":{\"k\":1,\"other\":1,\"extra\":2},\"reversed\":{\"k\":2,\"extra\":2,\"other\":1},\"explicit\":{\"k\":9,\"other\":1}}\n","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

`first_wins` has `k: 1` because `p` came first in the list, and `reversed` has `k: 2` for the same reason. Both have all three of `k`, `other`, and `extra`, since the merge adds keys that are missing. `explicit` has `k: 9`: the key written in the mapping itself overrides the merged one.

The merge is **shallow**. If the merged mapping contains a nested mapping or list and you set the same top-level key, the whole value is replaced, not combined:

```example
{"id":"yaml-anchors-06","title":"Merging is shallow","script":"cat > shallow.yaml <<'EOF'\ndefaults: &d\n  env: {A: 1}\n  tags: [x]\nover:\n  <<: *d\n  env: {B: 2}\nEOF\nyaml2json --yaml-1.1 shallow.yaml | jq -c .over\n","stdout":"{\"env\":{\"B\":2},\"tags\":[\"x\"]}\n","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-06.sh","truncated":false}
```

`over.env` is `{"B": 2}`. The `A: 1` from the defaults is gone, and `tags` was kept. If you need a deep merge, do it explicitly in code, or with `jq`'s `*` operator ([jq transforms](/lessons/jq-transform)).

## When to use them

Anchors earn their place when the same block repeats three or more times and must stay identical, such as the shared steps in a CI file or the common settings of several services. They cost readability: a reader has to scroll up to find what `*base` means, and an edit to the anchor changes every use. Two or three repeated lines are usually clearer written out. If a tool validates the file against a schema ([JSON Schema basics](/lessons/json-schema-basics)), validate the *resolved* data, because that is what the program will see.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id":"yaml-anchors-ex01","title":"Share a block of settings","prompt":"Write `services.yaml` with an anchored mapping `common` holding `restart: always` and `log: json`. Then define services `api` and `worker` that both merge `common`, and give `worker` its own `log: text`. Convert with `--yaml-1.1` and print the result with `jq -c`.","hint":"Use `<<: *common` as the first line inside each service, and write `log: text` after it.","hint2":"","solution":"`api` inherits both keys. `worker` inherits `restart` and overrides `log`, because an explicit key wins over a merged one.","script":"cat > services.yaml <<'EOF'\ncommon: &common\n  restart: always\n  log: json\napi:\n  <<: *common\n  port: 80\nworker:\n  <<: *common\n  log: text\nEOF\nyaml2json --yaml-1.1 services.yaml | jq -c '{api, worker}'\n","stdout":"{\"api\":{\"restart\":\"always\",\"log\":\"json\",\"port\":80},\"worker\":{\"restart\":\"always\",\"log\":\"text\"}}\n","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-ex01.sh"}
```

The inherited `image` key is not on `job` itself. It sits under the `<<` key, so a program that reads `job.image` would find nothing.","script":"cat > job.yaml <<'EOF'\ndefaults: &d\n  image: alpine\njob:\n  <<: *d\n  cmd: echo hi\nEOF\necho \"== 1.2\"; yaml2json job.yaml | jq -c .job\necho \"== 1.1\"; yaml2json --yaml-1.1 job.yaml | jq -c .job\n","stdout":"== 1.2\n{\"<<\":{\"image\":\"alpine\"},\"cmd\":\"echo hi\"}\n== 1.1\n{\"image\":\"alpine\",\"cmd\":\"echo hi\"}\n","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-anchors-ex02.sh"}

lessons.summary: A YAML file is a stream that can hold several documents. Learn the document markers, where comments are allowed, what a %YAML directive does, and how a parser treats tags it does not know.

lessons.pitfall: A generic YAML parser does not reject a tag it does not recognise. It drops the tag and keeps the value, so `!Ref MyBucket` loads as the plain string "MyBucket". Whatever the tag meant is lost without an error. A tool that needs the tag, such as CloudFormation, must be given a parser that knows it.
lessons.markdown:
A JSON file is one value. A YAML file is a **stream** of zero or more documents, and each document is one value. Most files have a single document, but multi-document files are routine: Kubernetes manifests and many log formats use them.

## Document markers

A line of three dashes, `---`, starts a document. A line of three dots, `...`, ends one. The start marker is optional for the first document and required to separate the rest. The end marker is rarely needed, since the next `---` also ends the previous document.

```example
{"id":"yaml-documents-01","title":"A stream of three documents","script":"cat > stream.yaml <<'EOF'
a: 1
---
b: 2
...
---
c: 3
EOF
echo "== without --all"
yaml2json stream.yaml || echo "(exit status $?)"
echo "== with --all"
yaml2json --all stream.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== yamlcheck"
yamlcheck stream.yaml
","stdout":"== without --all
(exit status 1)
== with --all
[{"a":1},{"b":2},{"c":3}]
== yamlcheck
stream.yaml: ok, 3 documents
","stderr":"stream.yaml: stream has 3 documents; pass --all
","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-documents-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

By default `yaml2json` refuses a stream with more than one document, because a single JSON value cannot hold three. `--all` collects them into a JSON array in order. `yamlcheck` counts them: three documents, with the `...` end marker making no difference to the count.

A JSON consumer cannot read a stream, so multi-document YAML is usually split first, or converted with `--all` and processed as an array. Lesson 19 does this with a Kubernetes-style file.

## Comments

A `#` starts a comment **only when it follows whitespace or begins a line**. Inside quotes, or glued to other text, it is just a character:

```example
{"id":"yaml-documents-02","title":"When a # is a comment","script":"cat > comments.yaml <<'EOF'
a: 1 # a comment
b: 2#not a comment
# a whole-line comment
c: "x # y"
EOF
yaml2json comments.yaml | jq -c .
","stdout":"{"a":1,"b":"2#not a comment","c":"x # y"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-documents-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

`a` is `1` with the comment stripped, `b` is the string `"2#not a comment"`, and `c` keeps the `#` inside the quotes. JSON has no comments at all, so converting to JSON discards them. They are not in the tree.

One practical habit follows from the stream rule. When you receive a YAML file from someone else, count its documents before assuming it is one value. `yamlcheck` prints the count, and a file that you expected to hold a single configuration but that reports two is usually a sign of a stray `---` in the middle of a copy-and-paste.

## Directives

A line beginning with `%` before the `---` is a **directive**. The one you will see is `%YAML`, which declares the YAML version of the document. A parser that supports several versions uses it to choose rules. Here the helper runs in its default 1.2 mode, yet the directive changes the outcome:

```example
{"id":"yaml-documents-03","title":"A %YAML directive changes how a document is read","script":"printf '%%YAML 1.2\n---\na: no\n' > v12.yaml
printf '%%YAML 1.1\n---\na: no\n' > v11.yaml
printf '%%YAML 1.3\n---\na: 1\n' > v13.yaml
echo "== declared 1.2"; yaml2json v12.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== declared 1.1"; yaml2json v11.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== declared 1.3"; yamlcheck v13.yaml
","stdout":"== declared 1.2
{"a":"no"}
== declared 1.1
{"a":false}
== declared 1.3
v13.yaml:1:7: BAD_DIRECTIVE: Unsupported YAML version 1.3 (warning)
v13.yaml: ok, 1 document
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-documents-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

Under `%YAML 1.1`, `no` became `false`, even though no `--yaml-1.1` flag was passed. This is the Norway problem from [lesson 11](/lessons/yaml-types), switched on by the file itself. A version the parser does not know, like 1.3, produced a `BAD_DIRECTIVE` warning from `yamlcheck`, and the document was still read.

Directives are rare in practice. Most files carry none, which means the version comes from the library that loads them.

## Tags

A **tag** says what type a node is, written before the value with `!`. YAML defines a set of standard tags, spelled `!!` followed by a name. The ones that matter: `!!str`, `!!int`, `!!float`, `!!bool`, `!!null`, and `!!binary`. Beyond those, anyone can define their own, such as `!Ref` and `!Sub` in AWS CloudFormation templates.

```example
{"id":"yaml-documents-04","title":"Core tags and tags the parser does not know","script":"cat > tags.yaml <<'EOF'
a: !!int "42"
b: !!str 42
c: !!bool "true"
d: !!null ""
e: !Ref MyBucket
f: !GetAtt [Res, Arn]
g: !Sub "x-${AWS::Region}"
EOF
yaml2json tags.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== yamlcheck"
yamlcheck tags.yaml
","stdout":"{"a":42,"b":"42","c":true,"d":null,"e":"MyBucket","f":["Res","Arn"],"g":"x-${AWS::Region}"}
== yamlcheck
tags.yaml:5:4: TAG_RESOLVE_FAILED: Unresolved tag: !Ref (warning)
tags.yaml:6:4: TAG_RESOLVE_FAILED: Unresolved tag: !GetAtt (warning)
tags.yaml:7:4: TAG_RESOLVE_FAILED: Unresolved tag: !Sub (warning)
tags.yaml: ok, 1 document
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-documents-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Read the output carefully:

- `!!int "42"` forced the quoted text to the number 42, and `!!str 42` forced the number to the string `"42"`. `!!bool "true"` and `!!null ""` converted the text in the same way. So a tag can *change* the type that guessing would pick, which is why `!!str` is the heavy-duty alternative to quoting.
- The three CloudFormation tags did not fail. `!Ref MyBucket` is the string `"MyBucket"`, `!GetAtt [Res, Arn]` is a list of two strings, and `!Sub` kept its text unchanged. **The tags are gone from the JSON.**
- `yamlcheck` reports a `TAG_RESOLVE_FAILED` warning for each of the three, and still says the document is fine. `yaml2json` printed nothing to stderr and exited 0. A warning is easy to miss, and a converter has no obligation to show it.

The consequence is the one in the pitfall above. A generic loader gives you the values but not the meaning, so a CloudFormation file converted this way no longer says which strings are references.

lessons.pitfall: A parser can be "safe" and still hand you data you did not expect. Safe loading answers "can this file run code or eat all my memory?". It does not answer "is `port` a number between 1 and 65535?". That second question is validation, and it is a separate step.
lessons.markdown:
Everything so far assumed you wrote the file. A YAML file that arrives from a user, a pull request, or an upload is **untrusted input**, and YAML needs more care than JSON here because it is a richer language. This lesson covers the specific ways it goes wrong and the small number of habits that prevent them.

## Risk 1: tags that build objects

A tag names a type, and some loaders let a tag name a *type in the host language*. This is a documented behaviour of PyYAML. Its full loader, `yaml.load` with an unsafe loader class, can construct arbitrary Python objects from tags such as `!!python/object/apply:...`, and that includes calling functions. For that reason PyYAML's documentation tells you to use `yaml.safe_load` for any input you do not control, which accepts only the standard YAML types. Treating `load` as an alias for `safe_load` is the classic mistake. Libraries in other languages that can build native objects from tags carry the same class of risk, so the advice is the same everywhere.

This course does not run such a payload. What we can show safely is what a *generic, safe* parser does with the same text:

```example
{"id":"yaml-safety-01","title":"A language-specific tag in a safe parser","script":"cat > payload.yaml <<'EOF'
!!python/object/apply:os.system ["echo hi"]
EOF
echo "== yaml2json"
yaml2json payload.yaml | jq -c .
echo "== yamlcheck"
yamlcheck payload.yaml
","stdout":"== yaml2json
["echo hi"]
== yamlcheck
payload.yaml:1:1: TAG_RESOLVE_FAILED: Unresolved tag: tag:yaml.org,2002:python/object/apply:os.system (warning)
payload.yaml: ok, 1 document
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-safety-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

The `yaml` package does not know a `python/object/apply` tag. It reported an unresolved tag, dropped it, and returned the argument list as plain data. Nothing was called, since this parser has no mechanism for constructing objects from tags. That is what "safe" means in practice: the document can only produce maps, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and nulls.

Rule one: use the safe entry point of whichever library you have, and never enable object construction for input you did not write.

## Risk 2: aliases that expand

Lesson 12 showed that an alias is a copy in JSON. That means a small document can describe a very large one. Here each level lists the previous level nine times:

```example
{"id":"yaml-safety-02","title":"A small file that describes a very large one","script":"cat > bomb.yaml <<'EOF'
a: &a ["lol","lol","lol","lol","lol","lol","lol","lol","lol"]
b: &b [*a,*a,*a,*a,*a,*a,*a,*a,*a]
c: &c [*b,*b,*b,*b,*b,*b,*b,*b,*b]
d: &d [*c,*c,*c,*c,*c,*c,*c,*c,*c]
e: &e [*d,*d,*d,*d,*d,*d,*d,*d,*d]
f: &f [*e,*e,*e,*e,*e,*e,*e,*e,*e]
EOF
printf 'source size: '; wc -c < bomb.yaml
echo "nine to the sixth power: $((9*9*9*9*9*9)) copies of \"lol\" under f"
yaml2json bomb.yaml || echo "(exit status $?)"
","stdout":"source size: 237
nine to the sixth power: 531441 copies of "lol" under f
(exit status 1)
","stderr":"bomb.yaml: Excessive alias count indicates a resource exhaustion attack
","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-safety-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

The file is 237 bytes, as the first line of output shows. Fully expanded, `f` alone holds 531441 strings. This is the "billion laughs" attack, and a parser that expands it naively can use gigabytes of memory.

The `yaml` package guards against this with a limit, `maxAliasCount`, and `yaml2json` exposes it as `--max-alias-count`. The default rejected the file above with a clear message. The same limit is useful in the other direction too: you can lower it for small, hand-written configs.

```example
{"id":"yaml-safety-03","title":"The alias limit, raised and lowered","script":"cat > small.yaml <<'EOF'
a: &a [x, x, x, x]
b: &b [*a, *a, *a, *a]
c: &c [*b, *b, *b, *b]
EOF
echo "== default limit"
yaml2json small.yaml | jq -c '.c | flatten | length'
echo "== limit 10"
yaml2json --max-alias-count 10 small.yaml || echo "(exit status $?)"
","stdout":"== default limit
64
== limit 10
(exit status 1)
","stderr":"small.yaml: Excessive alias count indicates a resource exhaustion attack
","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-safety-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

The 64 strings in `small.yaml` pass the default limit and fail a limit of 10. Pick a limit that is generous for your legitimate files and far from what an attacker would want. Other libraries have different defaults, or none. Check yours.

Size limits matter too, but they belong outside the parser: cap the upload size, and cap nesting depth if your loader exposes it.

## Risk 3: duplicate keys

A mapping with the same key twice is ambiguous. JSON's RFC says names SHOULD be unique and does not say what a parser must do, so different tools disagree. YAML 1.2 requires keys to be unique, and the `yaml` package reports an error:

```example
{"id":"yaml-safety-04","title":"Duplicate keys in YAML and in JSON","script":"printf 'role: user\nrole: admin\n' > dup.yaml
printf '{"role": "user", "role": "admin"}\n' > dup.json
echo "== YAML, yamlcheck"
yamlcheck dup.yaml || true
echo "== JSON text, read as YAML"
yamlcheck dup.json || true
echo "== JSON text, jq"
jq -c . dup.json
","stdout":"== YAML, yamlcheck
dup.yaml:2:1: DUPLICATE_KEY: Map keys must be unique
== JSON text, read as YAML
dup.json:1:18: DUPLICATE_KEY: Map keys must be unique
== JSON text, jq
{"role":"admin"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-safety-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

`yamlcheck` flagged both files, but `jq` printed `{"role":"admin"}` without complaint: the last value won. This is a security issue, not a style point. If one component validates the first value and another uses the last, an attacker can show each component a different answer. Rejecting duplicate keys at parse time closes that gap. For more on this see [JSON objects](/lessons/json-objects).

## The habit: safe parse, then validate

Safe loading tells you the data has the shape of plain maps and lists. It does not tell you the *contents* are right. Add a second step, which is to check the result against a schema, covered in [JSON Schema basics](/lessons/json-schema-basics):

```example
{"id":"yaml-safety-05","title":"Safe parse, then validate","script":"cat > schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["role", "port"],
  "properties": {
    "role": {"enum": ["user", "admin"]},
    "port": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 65535}
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}
EOF
printf 'role: user\nport: 8080\n' > good.yaml
printf 'role: root\nport: "8080"\nextra: true\n' > bad.yaml
schema-check schema.json good.yaml bad.yaml || echo "(exit status $?)"
","stdout":"good.yaml: valid
bad.yaml: (root) must NOT have additional properties 'extra'
bad.yaml: /role must be equal to one of the allowed values ["user","admin"]
bad.yaml: /port must be integer
(exit status 1)
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/yaml-safety-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

The good file passes. The bad one fails three checks at once: wrong role, a port that is a string, and an extra key. All three are things a safe parser accepts happily. The `|| echo` shows the exit status is non-zero, which is what a CI step or upload handler can act on.

Each step catches a different thing. The safe loader stops code execution, the alias limit stops memory exhaustion, the duplicate-key check stops two components disagreeing about one document, and the schema stops well-formed but wrong data. None of them replaces the others, and all four are cheap compared with an incident. If your language's YAML library cannot reject duplicate keys or cap aliases, put a small checker like `yamlcheck` in front of it in CI.

In short: use the safe loader, set resource limits, reject duplicate keys, validate the result, and only then use it.

lessons.title: JSON Schema, the basics
lessons.summary: A schema is a JSON document that says what other documents must look like. Write one, run it, and learn to read the errors.
objectives: Write a draft 2020-12 schema using type, properties, required, and additionalProperties
Constrain values with enum, const, minimum, maximum, minLength, pattern, items, and minItems
Read schema-check output, including which part of the data each message points at
Validate a YAML file against a schema written in JSON
lessons.pitfall: Unless a schema says `required`, a property may be missing. Unless it says `additionalProperties: false`, unknown properties are accepted. A schema that lists only `properties` therefore accepts `{}` and also `{"prot": 80}`, a misspelt port. Most "the schema passed but the config is wrong" reports are one of these two omissions.
lessons.markdown:
A parser answers one question: is this text well-formed? It cannot tell you that `port` should be a number between 1 and 65535, or that `environment` must be one of three names. **JSON Schema** answers that second question. A schema is itself a JSON document. A validator reads the schema and a data document and reports every place where the data breaks the rules.

Schemas apply to the tree from [the first lesson](/lessons/one-data-model), not to the text. That is why a JSON Schema can validate a YAML file: parse the YAML into a tree, then validate the tree.

## A first schema

The course helper `schema-check` uses Ajv, which implements draft 2020-12 and asserts `format` keywords through the `ajv-formats` plugin. It prints one line per problem and exits 0 only when every file is valid.

```example
{"id":"json-schema-basics-01","title":"A schema for a small service description","script":"cat > service.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
    "port": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 65535},
    "env":  {"enum": ["dev", "staging", "prod"]}
  },
  "required": ["name", "port"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
EOF
cat > good.json <<'EOF'
{"name": "api", "port": 8080, "env": "prod"}
EOF
schema-check service.schema.json good.json
echo "exit status: $?"
","stdout":"good.json: valid
exit status: 0
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-basics-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

Every keyword is a small test, and a document must pass all of them. `type` checks the kind of value. `properties` attaches a sub-schema to each named key. `required` lists keys that must be present. `additionalProperties: false` rejects any key not named in `properties`. `enum` lists the allowed values.

## Reading the errors

With `allErrors` turned on, the validator reports every failure rather than stopping at the first. Each line is `file`, then a JSON Pointer to the offending part of the data, then the message. `(root)` means the whole document, and `/port` means the `port` key.

```example
{"id":"json-schema-basics-02","title":"One bad document, several messages","script":"cat > service.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
    "port": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 65535},
    "env":  {"enum": ["dev", "staging", "prod"]}
  },
  "required": ["name", "port"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
EOF
cat > bad.json <<'EOF'
{"port": 70000, "env": "production", "colour": "blue"}
EOF
schema-check service.schema.json bad.json
","stdout":"bad.json: (root) must have required property 'name'
bad.json: (root) must NOT have additional properties 'colour'
bad.json: /port must be <= 65535
bad.json: /env must be equal to one of the allowed values ["dev","staging","prod"]
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-basics-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

Four problems, four lines. The message for `additionalProperties` names the offending key, and the message for `enum` lists the allowed values. A pointer such as `/items/2/qty` means "key `items`, element 2, key `qty`", counting from zero.

## Validating YAML

The tree is what gets validated, so the data file can be YAML. `schema-check` parses files ending in `.yaml` or `.yml` as YAML 1.2 first. The same schema file serves both formats.

```example
{"id":"json-schema-basics-03","title":"The same schema, a YAML document","script":"cat > service.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": {"type": "string"},
    "port": {"type": "integer"}
  },
  "required": ["name", "port"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
EOF
cat > svc.yaml <<'EOF'
name: api
port: "8080"
EOF
schema-check service.schema.json svc.yaml
","stdout":"svc.yaml: /port must be integer
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-basics-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

The string `"8080"` is not an integer, even though it looks like one. Quoting made it a string in the tree, and the schema checks the tree. Under YAML's own rules the unquoted `port: 8080` would have been a number.

## More constraints

Strings, numbers, and arrays each have their own keywords:

| Keyword | Applies to | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `minLength`, `maxLength` | string | Length in characters |
| `pattern` | string | A regular expression that may match anywhere in the string unless anchored with `^` and `$` |
| `minimum`, `maximum` | number | Inclusive bounds. `exclusiveMinimum` and `exclusiveMaximum` are strict |
| `multipleOf` | number | The value must be a whole multiple |
| `items` | array | A schema every element must satisfy |
| `minItems`, `maxItems`, `uniqueItems` | array | Size and uniqueness |
| `const` | any | Exactly one allowed value |
| `format` | string | Named shapes such as `email`, `uri`, `date`, `uuid` |

```example
{"id":"json-schema-basics-04","title":"Arrays, patterns, and formats","script":"cat > team.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "version": {"const": 1},
    "slug":    {"type": "string", "pattern": "^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$"},
    "contact": {"type": "string", "format": "email"},
    "members": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "minItems": 2, "uniqueItems": true}
  },
  "required": ["version", "slug", "members"]
}
EOF
cat > team.yaml <<'EOF'
version: 2
slug: Platform Team
contact: not-an-email
members: [ada]
EOF
schema-check team.schema.json team.yaml
","stdout":"team.yaml: /version must be equal to constant
team.yaml: /slug must match pattern "^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$"
team.yaml: /contact must match format "email"
team.yaml: /members must NOT have fewer than 2 items
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-basics-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Without `ajv-formats`, many validators treat `format` as a comment and accept anything. Draft 2020-12 allows that, so a schema that relies on `format` is only as strict as the validator running it. Check yours with a deliberately bad value, as above.

## What a schema cannot do

A schema checks the shape of one document. It cannot check that a `port` is free on the host, that two services do not share a name unless you write `uniqueItems` for that, or that a referenced file exists. It also does not *fix* anything: validation never fills in defaults or converts types. Lesson 16 returns to that.

objectives: Factor repeated shapes into $defs and refer to them with $ref
Choose between allOf, anyOf, oneOf, and not

lessons.pitfall: `additionalProperties` only looks at the `properties` that sit beside it in the same schema object. It cannot see properties declared inside an `allOf` branch, so combining the two rejects keys that every branch accepts. Use `unevaluatedProperties` when you extend a base schema.
lessons.markdown:
[Lesson 15](/lessons/json-schema-basics) wrote one flat schema. Real contracts repeat themselves: every service has a port, every environment has a name. Draft 2020-12 gives you ways to name a piece once and reuse it, and ways to combine pieces.

## $defs and $ref

`$defs` is a holding area for named sub-schemas. `$ref` points at one with a JSON Pointer, so `#/$defs/port` means "the `port` entry under `$defs` in this document".

```example
{"id":"json-schema-composition-01","title":"One definition, used twice","script":"cat > pair.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$defs": {
    "port": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 65535}
  },
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "listen": {"$ref": "#/$defs/port"},
    "admin":  {"$ref": "#/$defs/port"}
  },
  "required": ["listen"]
}
EOF
printf 'listen: 8080\nadmin: 99999\n' > pair.yaml
schema-check pair.schema.json pair.yaml
","stdout":"pair.yaml: /admin must be <= 65535
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-composition-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

The error points at `/admin`, the place in the data, not at the definition. The rule lives in one spot, so changing the maximum changes both properties.

## allOf, anyOf, oneOf, not

| Keyword | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| `allOf` | every sub-schema passes |
| `anyOf` | at least one passes |
| `oneOf` | exactly one passes |
| `not` | the sub-schema fails |

`oneOf` is the usual source of confusion. If two branches both match, `oneOf` fails, and the message says so.

```example
{"id":"json-schema-composition-02","title":"oneOf fails when two branches match","script":"cat > source.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "oneOf": [
    {"type": "object", "required": ["url"]},
    {"type": "object", "required": ["path"]}
  ]
}
EOF
echo '{"url": "https://example.com"}'                > url.json
echo '{"url": "https://example.com", "path": "/tmp"}' > both.json
echo '{}'                                            > neither.json
schema-check source.schema.json url.json both.json neither.json
","stdout":"url.json: valid
both.json: (root) must match exactly one schema in oneOf
neither.json: (root) must have required property 'url'
neither.json: (root) must have required property 'path'
neither.json: (root) must match exactly one schema in oneOf
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-composition-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

A document with only `url` matches the first branch and not the second, so it passes. With both keys it matches two branches, and the only message is `must match exactly one schema in oneOf`. With neither it matches none, and you also get one line per branch explaining why that branch failed (`url` missing, `path` missing) before the closing `oneOf` line. So the two failures look different: when you see only the `oneOf` line, too many branches matched, and when you see per-branch lines, none did. If you meant "at least one", write `anyOf`.

`not` inverts a sub-schema and is mostly useful for forbidding a value, for example `{"not": {"const": "root"}}` on a `user` property. Because the error can only say that the inner schema matched, prefer a positive rule such as `enum` when you can.

## if / then / else

Some rules depend on another field: a `tls` section is needed only when `scheme` is `https`. `if` is tested against the data. If it passes, `then` applies; otherwise `else` does. A failing `if` is not an error by itself.

```example
{"id":"json-schema-composition-03","title":"A rule that applies only when scheme is https","script":"cat > endpoint.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {"scheme": {"enum": ["http", "https"]}},
  "required": ["scheme"],
  "if": {"properties": {"scheme": {"const": "https"}}},
  "then": {"required": ["cert"]}
}
EOF
printf 'scheme: http\n'              > plain.yaml
printf 'scheme: https\ncert: a.pem\n' > secure.yaml
printf 'scheme: https\n'             > nocert.yaml
schema-check endpoint.schema.json plain.yaml secure.yaml nocert.yaml
","stdout":"plain.yaml: valid
secure.yaml: valid
nocert.yaml: (root) must have required property 'cert'
nocert.yaml: (root) must match "then" schema
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-composition-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

## additionalProperties and allOf

Suppose you extend a base shape with another. It looks natural to close the result with `additionalProperties: false`.

```example
{"id":"json-schema-composition-04","title":"additionalProperties cannot see inside allOf","script":"cat > closed.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "allOf": [
    {"properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}}},
    {"properties": {"port": {"type": "integer"}}}
  ],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
EOF
cat > open.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "allOf": [
    {"properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}}},
    {"properties": {"port": {"type": "integer"}}}
  ],
  "unevaluatedProperties": false
}
EOF
printf 'name: api\nport: 80\n'            > fine.yaml
printf 'name: api\nport: 80\nextra: 1\n'  > extra.yaml
echo "--- additionalProperties"
schema-check closed.schema.json fine.yaml extra.yaml || true
echo "--- unevaluatedProperties"
schema-check open.schema.json fine.yaml extra.yaml
","stdout":"--- additionalProperties
fine.yaml: (root) must NOT have additional properties 'name'
fine.yaml: (root) must NOT have additional properties 'port'
extra.yaml: (root) must NOT have additional properties 'name'
extra.yaml: (root) must NOT have additional properties 'port'
extra.yaml: (root) must NOT have additional properties 'extra'
--- unevaluatedProperties
fine.yaml: valid
extra.yaml: (root) must NOT have unevaluated properties
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-composition-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Read the first block of output carefully. `additionalProperties` sees no `properties` beside it, so every key counts as additional, and the perfectly good `fine.yaml` is rejected. `unevaluatedProperties` instead asks which keys *any* keyword in the schema has already handled, so `name` and `port` are accepted and `extra.yaml` is the only file rejected. Note that its message, `must NOT have unevaluated properties`, does not name the key the way the `additionalProperties` message does, so you have to find the extra key yourself.

The rule of thumb: use `additionalProperties: false` in a flat schema where `properties` is right beside it, and `unevaluatedProperties: false` at the top of a schema that uses `allOf`, `$ref`, or `if/then/else` to build the shape. Ajv's strict mode also asks for `"type": "object"` beside either keyword, which is why both schemas above declare it.

## Validation does not apply defaults

A schema can say `"default": 8080`. That keyword is an annotation, a hint for tools that generate forms or documentation. It does not insert anything into the data, and it does not make a missing required key valid.

```example
{"id":"json-schema-composition-05","title":"default does not rescue a missing key","script":"cat > def.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {"port": {"type": "integer", "default": 8080}},
  "required": ["port"]
}
EOF
echo '{}' > empty.json
schema-check def.schema.json empty.json
","stdout":"empty.json: (root) must have required property 'port'
","stderr":"","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/json-schema-composition-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

If your program needs a default, apply it in code after validating. Ajv has an optional `useDefaults` setting that fills them in, but `schema-check` does not enable it, and a contract that quietly rewrites its input is harder to reason about than one that only reports.

## A habit for larger schemas

Build up a schema one keyword at a time and keep a small set of files that should pass and a set that should fail. After each change, run `schema-check` against both sets. A schema you have only seen accept good data may be accepting everything, as the lesson 15 pitfall showed. Putting the failing examples in version control next to the schema is the cheapest regression test a contract can have, and [the capstone](/lessons/capstone) does exactly that.

## Pointing an editor at a schema

Editors can validate as you type. The YAML language server, used by the Red Hat YAML extension for VS Code, reads a modeline comment at the top of a YAML file:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=./service.schema.json
name: api
port: 8080
```

That comment is an editor feature. A YAML parser treats it as a comment, so the data is unchanged and nothing validates unless the editor or a command such as `schema-check` runs.

lessons.pitfall: A round trip that "works" on your test file can still lose information. Conversion is safe only for the part of YAML that JSON can already express. Comments, anchors, tags, and non-string keys are gone after one pass through JSON, and nothing in the output tells you they were there.
lessons.markdown:
Converting is mostly a question of which direction you go. JSON is the smaller format, so every JSON document has a YAML spelling. YAML is the larger one, so a conversion to JSON has to throw something away. This lesson captures what.

## Losses going to JSON

A small YAML file with a comment, an anchor, a tag, and a second document shows most of it. `yaml2json` refuses a stream of several documents unless you pass `--all`.

```example
{"id":"converting-01","title":"A comment, an anchor, and a second document","script":"cat > multi.yaml <<'EOF'
# deployment defaults
defaults: &d
  retries: 3   # per request
service:
  <<: *d
  name: api
copy: *d
---
second: true
EOF
yaml2json multi.yaml
","stdout":"","stderr":"multi.yaml: stream has 2 documents; pass --all
","exitCode":1,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

The tool stops and says the stream has two documents. JSON has no way to hold two documents in one file. With `--all` the result is an array of trees, which is a choice the tool made, not something YAML specifies.

```example
{"id":"converting-02","title":"One document, comments and anchors gone","script":"cat > one.yaml <<'EOF'
# deployment defaults
defaults: &d
  retries: 3   # per request
copy: *d
EOF
yaml2json one.yaml
echo "--- and back to YAML ---"
yaml2json one.yaml | json2yaml
","stdout":"{
  "defaults": {
    "retries": 3
  },
  "copy": {
    "retries": 3
  }
}
--- and back to YAML ---
defaults:
  retries: 3
copy:
  retries: 3
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

Both comments disappeared. `copy` became a full duplicate of `defaults` instead of a reference, and the way back does not restore the alias: the second YAML file has the same data, spelled out twice. If somebody edits `retries` under `defaults` in that file, `copy` no longer follows. The anchor was information about *how the author wrote it*, not about the data, and JSON has no place for it.

## Several documents

`--all` is the way through. It prints one JSON array holding one tree per document, and `jq` can then take the array apart again, one compact line per document.

```example
{"id":"converting-03","title":"A document stream as a JSON array","script":"cat > stream.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Service
name: api
---
kind: Job
name: migrate
EOF
yaml2json --all stream.yaml | jq -c '.[]'
echo "--- just the names ---"
yaml2json --all stream.yaml | jq -r '.[].name'
","stdout":"{"kind":"Service","name":"api"}
{"kind":"Job","name":"migrate"}
--- just the names ---
api
migrate
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

The array is a convention of this helper. A tool that reads a stream may instead emit one JSON value per line, which is the [JSON Lines](/lessons/json-lines) format, so check what a converter does with a stream before you build on it.

## Tags and keys

Tags are another thing a JSON tree cannot carry. Non-string keys are a third, because a JSON object key is always a string.

```example
{"id":"converting-04","title":"Tags and unusual keys through the converter","script":"cat > odd.yaml <<'EOF'
count: !!str 12
ref: !Ref MyBucket
1: one
true: "yes"
? [a, b]
: pair
null: nothing
EOF
yaml2json odd.yaml
","stdout":"{
  "1": "one",
  "count": "12",
  "ref": "MyBucket",
  "true": "yes",
  "[ a, b ]": "pair",
  "": "nothing"
}
","stderr":"(node:21216) Warning: Keys with collection values will be stringified due to JS Object restrictions: "[ a, b ]". Set mapAsMap: true to use object keys.
(Use `node --trace-warnings ...` to show where the warning was created)
","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

Read the output slowly. The explicit `!!str` tag made `12` a string, which survived because JSON has strings. The `!Ref` tag, which AWS CloudFormation uses, was silently dropped and only the word `MyBucket` remains. The integer key `1` and the boolean key `true` became the strings `"1"` and `"true"`. The list key `[a, b]` was flattened into the string `[ a, b ]`, and Node printed a warning on stderr saying so. The key `null` became the empty string `""`. None of those conversions fail, and none changes the exit status. If your data has keys like these, check the output by eye.

## JSON to YAML is safe, with one catch

Going the other way you start from the smaller format, so nothing can be lost. The catch is how the YAML is *written*. `json2yaml` uses the `yaml` package, which targets YAML 1.2, and only quotes a string when a 1.2 reader would otherwise read it as something else.

```example
{"id":"converting-05","title":"Strings that a YAML 1.1 reader would change","script":"cat > strings.json <<'EOF'
{"country": "no", "switch": "on", "mode": "010", "ratio": "1:30", "flag": "true", "version": "3.10"}
EOF
json2yaml strings.json | tee strings.yaml
echo "--- read as YAML 1.2 ---"
yaml2json strings.yaml
echo "--- read as YAML 1.1 ---"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 strings.yaml
","stdout":"country: no
switch: on
mode: "010"
ratio: 1:30
flag: "true"
version: "3.10"
--- read as YAML 1.2 ---
{
  "country": "no",
  "switch": "on",
  "mode": "010",
  "ratio": "1:30",
  "flag": "true",
  "version": "3.10"
}
--- read as YAML 1.1 ---
{
  "country": false,
  "switch": true,
  "mode": "010",
  "ratio": 90,
  "flag": "true",
  "version": "3.10"
}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

Compare the three outputs. `json2yaml` quoted `"010"`, `"true"`, and `"3.10"`, but left `no`, `on`, and `1:30` bare. A YAML 1.2 reader gets the original strings back. A YAML 1.1 reader turns `no` into `false`, `on` into `true`, and `1:30` into the number `90`. Both readers are correct for their version. The practical rule: if you write YAML that another team's tool will load, quote any string that could be a boolean, a number, or a time, whatever your own writer does. [Lesson 11](/lessons/yaml-types) lists the cases.

## Comparing as trees

When you test a conversion, compare trees, not text. Two files that differ only in key order or whitespace describe the same data. `jq -S` sorts object keys and prints in a fixed layout, so `diff` shows only real differences.

```example
{"id":"converting-06","title":"Canonical comparison with jq -S","script":"cat > a.json <<'EOF'
{"b": [1, 2], "a": {"y": 1, "x": 2}}
EOF
cat > b.yaml <<'EOF'
a:
  x: 2
  y: 1
b: [1, 2]
EOF
yaml2json b.yaml | jq -S . > b.canonical
jq -S . a.json > a.canonical
diff a.canonical b.canonical && echo "same tree"
echo "--- a real difference ---"
echo '{"a": {"x": 2, "y": 1}, "b": [2, 1]}' | jq -S . > c.canonical
diff a.canonical c.canonical || true
","stdout":"same tree
--- a real difference ---
7,8c7,8
<     1,
<     2
---
>     2,
>     1
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-06.sh","truncated":false}
```

Arrays are ordered, so `[1, 2]` and `[2, 1]` differ, and `diff` reports it. Objects are not, so `jq -S` is allowed to reorder keys.

## A conversion checklist

Before you rely on a YAML to JSON step in a pipeline, ask five questions. Does the file contain more than one document? Does anything depend on an anchor staying a shared reference rather than a copy? Are there tags the downstream tool needs? Are all keys plain strings? And do any bare words, such as `no`, `on`, or version numbers, need quoting for the *next* reader? A "no" to all five means the round trip is lossless.

The `!!str` tag is gone too, but the value stays the string `"1"` because the converter had already resolved it.","script":"cat > in.yaml <<'EOF'

```exercise
base: &b {os: linux}
ci: *b
v: !!str 1
EOF
yaml2json in.yaml | tee out.json
json2yaml out.json
","stdout":"{
  "base": {
    "os": "linux"
  },
  "ci": {
    "os": "linux"
  },
  "v": "1"
}
base:
  os: linux
ci:
  os: linux
v: "1"
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-ex01.sh"}
```

```exercise
{"id":"converting-ex02","title":"Make YAML safe for a 1.1 reader","prompt":"Take `{"answer": "yes", "region": "no"}`, produce YAML with `json2yaml`, then edit it so that a YAML 1.1 reader also gets strings. Prove it with `yaml2json --yaml-1.1`.","hint":"Quote the values by hand. Single or double quotes both work.","hint2":"","solution":"Quoting `"yes"` and `"no"` turns them into strings for either version, so the 1.1 read matches the 1.2 read.","script":"echo '{"answer": "yes", "region": "no"}' | json2yaml > raw.yaml
cat raw.yaml
echo "--- 1.1 read of the raw file ---"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 raw.yaml
printf 'answer: "yes"\nregion: "no"\n' > safe.yaml
echo "--- 1.1 read of the quoted file ---"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 safe.yaml
","stdout":"answer: yes
region: no
--- 1.1 read of the raw file ---
{
  "answer": true,
  "region": false
}
--- 1.1 read of the quoted file ---
{
  "answer": "yes",
  "region": "no"
}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/converting-ex02.sh"}
```

lessons.markdown:
GitHub Actions workflows live in `.github/workflows/*.yml`. They are the most common YAML file a developer edits, so they make a good test of everything so far. The file is parsed into a tree, and GitHub reads that tree: `on` says when to run, `jobs` is a mapping of job names, and each job has `runs-on` and a list of `steps`.

## The anatomy as a tree

The easiest way to see the structure is to convert a workflow to JSON.

```example
{"id":"github-actions-01","title":"A workflow and the tree behind it","script":"cat > ci.yml <<'EOF'
name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install
        run: npm ci
      - name: Test
        run: npm test
EOF
yaml2json ci.yml | jq -c '{name, on, jobs: (.jobs | keys), steps: (.jobs.test.steps | length)}'
yaml2json ci.yml | jq -c '.jobs.test.steps[]'
","stdout":"{"name":"ci","on":{"push":{"branches":["main"]},"pull_request":null},"jobs":["test"],"steps":3}
{"uses":"actions/checkout@v4"}
{"name":"Install","run":"npm ci"}
{"name":"Test","run":"npm test"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/github-actions-01.sh","truncated":false}
```

Each step is a mapping. `uses` names a reusable action, `run` holds a shell command, `name` is a label, and `with` supplies arguments. A step needs `uses` or `run`, not both. Notice `pull_request:` with nothing after it. An empty value is `null` in YAML, and GitHub accepts that as "run on every pull request event".

## The key called on

In YAML 1.1, the bare words `on`, `off`, `yes`, and `no` are booleans, so a 1.1 loader reads the key `on:` as `true`. In YAML 1.2 they are plain strings. GitHub's own parser reads `on` as the string, so the file works there, but another tool might not agree.

```example
{"id":"github-actions-02","title":"The same key under YAML 1.2 and 1.1","script":"cat > trigger.yml <<'EOF'
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
EOF
echo "--- YAML 1.2 ---"
yaml2json trigger.yml | jq -c 'keys'
echo "--- YAML 1.1 ---"
yaml2json --yaml-1.1 trigger.yml | jq -c 'keys'
","stdout":"--- YAML 1.2 ---
["on"]
--- YAML 1.1 ---
["true"]
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/github-actions-02.sh","truncated":false}
```

If a script of yours loads workflows with a 1.1 library, it will look for a `"on"` key and find `"true"`. The fix is in your script, not in the workflow: either use a 1.2 parser or handle both spellings. Writing `"on":` with quotes in the workflow also works on both, but most people leave it bare.

## Expressions are strings

`${{ ... }}` is GitHub's expression syntax. YAML does not know about it, so the parser sees an ordinary scalar, and the dollar sign and braces are legal inside a plain scalar when it starts with `$`. A value that *starts* with `{` would be a different story: YAML would try to read a flow mapping.

```example
{"id":"github-actions-03","title":"Quoting values that look like YAML syntax","script":"cat > quote.yml <<'EOF'
env:
  PLAIN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}
  FROM_BRACE: "{{ not.an.expression }}"
  GLOB: "*.js"
  RATIO: "3:1"
  BRANCHES: ['*', 'release/**']
EOF
yaml2json quote.yml
echo "--- the same glob, unquoted ---"
printf 'files: *.js\n' > unquoted-glob.yml
yaml2json unquoted-glob.yml || true
echo "--- braces at the start of a value, unquoted ---"
printf 'x: {{ a.b }}\n' > unquoted-brace.yml
yaml2json unquoted-brace.yml 2>/dev/null
","stdout":"{
  "env": {
    "PLAIN": "${{ secrets.TOKEN }}",
    "FROM_BRACE": "{{ not.an.expression }}",
    "GLOB": "*.js",
    "RATIO": "3:1",
    "BRANCHES": [
      "*",
      "release/**"
    ]
  }
}
--- the same glob, unquoted ---
--- braces at the start of a value, unquoted ---
{
  "x": {
    "{ a.b }": null
  }
}
","stderr":"unquoted-glob.yml: Unresolved alias (the anchor must be set before the alias): .js
","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/github-actions-03.sh","truncated":false}
```

A leading `*` starts an alias in YAML, so the unquoted glob is an error: the parser looks for an anchor named `.js` and finds none. Quoting `'*'` is the standard answer. The unquoted `{{ a.b }}` is worse because it is *not* an error. A value that starts with `{` is read as a flow mapping, so `x` becomes a mapping with one key, `{ a.b }`, whose value is null. The file parses and the meaning is wrong. GitHub's `${{ }}` form avoids this because the value starts with `$`, but a bare `{{ }}` copied from a templating language does not. The `:` in a plain scalar is only special when followed by a space, which is why `3:1` can be left bare, but quoting it makes the intent clear.

(`yamlcheck`, the course's checker, reports `unquoted-glob.yml` as fine, because it only looks at parse errors and the alias problem appears when the data is built. `yaml2json` builds the data, so it catches it. Run the converter as well when you want to be sure.)

## Multi-line commands

For anything longer than one line, use a literal block scalar (`|`). Every line is kept exactly, including newlines, and the shell receives it as one script.

```example
{"id":"github-actions-04","title":"run: | keeps newlines, run: > folds them","script":"cat > steps.yml <<'EOF'
steps:
  - run: |
      echo one
      echo two
  - run: >
      echo three
      echo four
EOF
yaml2json steps.yml | jq -c '.steps[].run'
","stdout":""echo one\necho two\n"
"echo three echo four\n"
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/github-actions-04.sh","truncated":false}
```

The first command is two lines, and the second is one line, because `>` folds line breaks into spaces. For a shell script you almost always want `|`. See [lesson 10](/lessons/yaml-scalars) for the chomping indicators that control the final newline.

## needs and if

Jobs run in parallel unless one names another in `needs`. A step or job can carry an `if` condition, which is again a string that GitHub evaluates later.

```example
{"id":"github-actions-05","title":"needs is a list, if is a string","script":"cat > flow.yml <<'EOF'
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: make
  deploy:
    needs: [build]
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: make deploy
EOF
yaml2json flow.yml | jq -c '.jobs.deploy | {needs, "if": .["if"], type_of_if: (.["if"] | type)}'
","stdout":"{"needs":["build"],"if":"github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'","type_of_if":"string"}
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/github-actions-05.sh","truncated":false}
```

The `if` value is a string to the parser, as the `type_of_if` field shows. Inside it, the single quotes belong to GitHub's expression language, and YAML passes them through untouched. Because a plain scalar cannot start with certain characters, an `if` that begins with `!` or `{` must be quoted or wrapped in `${{ }}`.

## Matrices

A matrix is a mapping from a name to a list of values, and GitHub runs the job once per combination.

```example
{"id":"github-actions-06","title":"A matrix is a mapping of lists, and a schema can check the shape","script":"cat > matrix.yml <<'EOF'
name: build
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        node: [20, 22]
    steps:
      - run: node --version
EOF
yaml2json matrix.yml | jq -c '.jobs.build.strategy.matrix'
cat > mini.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["on", "jobs"],
  "properties": {
    "jobs": {
      "type": "object",
      "minProperties": 1,
      "additionalProperties": {
        "type": "object",
        "required": ["runs-on"],
        "properties": {
          "steps": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {
              "type": "object",
              "anyOf": [{"required": ["uses"]}, {"required": ["run"]}]
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
EOF
schema-check mini.schema.json matrix.yml
printf 'on: push\njobs:\n  t:\n    steps:\n      - name: nothing\n' > broken.yml
schema-check mini.schema.json broken.yml || true
","stdout":"{"os":["ubuntu-latest","macos-latest"],"node":[20,22]}
matrix.yml: valid
broken.yml: /jobs/t must have required property 'runs-on'
broken.yml: /jobs/t/steps/0 must have required property 'uses'
broken.yml: /jobs/t/steps/0 must have required property 'run'
broken.yml: /jobs/t/steps/0 must match a schema in anyOf
","stderr":"","exitCode":0,"download":"/downloads/examples/github-actions-06.sh","truncated":false}
```

The schema above is a small hand-written one for this lesson, not GitHub's own. It checks that `on` and `jobs` exist, that every job has `runs-on`, and that every step has `uses` or `run`. It catches structural slips, but not a misspelt expression or a wrong action name. For fuller checking, use a dedicated workflow linter.
